object_text: The cosmos is a held breath: the world exists because a dead titan-god, Vurum, exhales in its sleep beneath the middle sea. Every breath-cycle (~400 years) it partially wakes, and the tide of souls that animates all living things reverses direction — the dead rise briefly toward the surface to rejoin the living flow. Civilization is built on the superstition that certain stone towers (the Nine Anchors) hammer the seabed to keep Vurum sleeping longer. What is already breaking: the northernmost Anchor, Karst-One, has cracked, and its region's dead no longer rise on schedule — they linger, unclaimed, feeding something that is now growing under the anchor's foundations.

dmml:proposes/origin: The Nine Anchors are not built stone at all — they are Vurum's own teeth, wrenched from its jaw by its nine children in the first act (the world's origin is a family murder, not an accident). Each tooth-root still remembers drawing soul-tide through a titan's body, which is why the Anchors hold the breath at all: they hammer the seabed with borrowed appetite. This makes the Karst-One crack theologically worse than a broken tower: the Firstborn jailer stationed there, Orrhun-Karst, has gone silent and is suspected of having pried the crack wider on purpose — the children are said to be able to inherit only if the parent dies awake. So the "something growing under the foundations" may be a sibling, not a stranger, and the lingering dead are being filed like teeth marks.

dmml:proposes/law: The one true prohibition follows from the breath itself: it is forbidden to keep a corpse past its rise-window. Because the dead ride the tide upward on Vurum's exhale-cycle, every household, temple, and crypt holds its dead in trust only until the next cycle-tide — the buriers' guilds (the Mandrel Houses) are paid precisely to give bodies back on schedule. Holding a dead body past its tide is the gravest crime, called "second theft," because a held soul is stolen from the living flow and must draw breath from somewhere — the family that withholds a grandmother's body for grief is literally taking breath from the living, which is why grief-murders spike in the generations after a bad tide. This law gives the mythographer's claim its teeth: Orrhun-Karst's crime, if he pried the crack wide, is second theft at geological scale — he is holding the tide itself past its window, and the thing growing under Karst-One is a hoarder with no room left in its lungs.

dmml:proposes/cosmology: Every exhale needs an exit, and the breath-cycle has one: the Gullet, a ring of nine brackish maelstroms in the middle sea where the soul-tide drains back down into Vurum between cycles. The Nine Anchors were driven in a ring precisely because they stand on the Gullet's rim — the teeth are hammered into the jaw-line of the mouth itself. This closes the law of second theft's open loop: a held corpse past its rise-window is a soul that never reaches the Gullet, and the Mandrel Houses' true job is not burial but *delivery* — they ship the dead downriver to the nearest Gullet-mouth on tide-days, which is why their toll-booths (the Mandrel locks, black wood studded with tooth-ivory) sit at every rivermouth. What is already breaking: with Karst-One cracked, the northern Gullet has slowed — it now takes three tide-days instead of one to swallow — so the north is developing a backlog of undelivered dead, and the Mandrel Houses have begun quietly paying families to keep bodies *longer*, inverting the one true prohibition in the only region where the law has visibly failed. The lawgiver's grief-murder spike and the mythographer's sibling-under-the-foundations are both downstream of the same blocked drain.

dmml:proposes/origin: The children who pulled Vurum's teeth are always counted as nine, but the oldest tally-songs count ten — and the tenth child, Sereth, was thrown into the Gullet by her siblings immediately after the murder, not for treachery but for witness: she was the one whose scream woke Vurum to the pain, and a parent cannot be left to die awake with a witness alive to name the killers. The Gullet's ring of nine maelstroms is not nine teeth in a jaw-line; it is eight teeth and one open mouth — the ninth maelstrom is Sereth's still-open throat, and that is why the northern drain has always been the slowest and why its slowing went unnoticed until Karst-One cracked. The moon is what remains of Sereth above the water: a single eye the tide dragged back up on the first exhale, which is why every exhale-cycle the moon swells with the rising dead — she is still counting them out, and someday the tally will be complete enough for her to name her siblings, one maelstrom at a time. This gives Orrhun-Karst a motive the family-murder account was missing: he does not want to inherit — he wants to finish Sereth's testimony, and cracking the Anchor was his first word.

dmml:proposes/law: The north's inversion cannot stand as mere lawlessness; write what it actually becomes. The Mandrel Houses' payments to hold bodies past the tide — the "salt-stay clause," a contract signed in brine and tooth-ivory at the rivermouth locks — do not suspend the law of second theft, they privatize it. A family that takes salt-stay money is no longer a household in grief; legally it becomes a Gullet, a private drain that swallows and does not release, and the soul it holds must draw breath from the family's own lungs — which is why salt-stay households suffer a recognizable wasting: the living thin out, breathe shallow, die early, and their own dead are then the next bodies held. Second theft has never had a punishment because it was unthinkable; salt-stay makes it an economy, so the law must name the penalty: a salt-stay taker forfeits their own rise-window — when they die, the Mandrel Houses are forbidden to deliver them to the Gullet, and they join the backlog, the first souls legally sentenced to the hoard under Karst-One. This is the trap the Houses have built for themselves: every toll-keeper who signs a salt-stay clause has signed away their own afterlife, and the backlog under Karst-One is being filled with the very guild sworn to empty it. This also sharpens Orrhun-Karst's crime: he is not merely a thief at geological scale, he is the precedent — the first salt-stay taker, holding the whole northern tide, and the sibling the mythographer suspects is growing under the foundations is being fed by guild-men who each believed they were only delaying one grandmother.

dmml:proposes/history: The breath has already slipped once. Roughly one cycle ago — four hundred years back, within written memory — Vurum half-woke during an exhale, and the event is not myth but ruin: the Second Breath. For nine days the soul-tide ran backwards, and the entire drowned coastal shelf of Old Amsel (now the sunken terraces visible at low tide off the middle sea's western rim) came apart when its own dead stood up inside it mid-act. What survives is material, not legend: the Amsel Reefs are its buildings, overgrown with the only coral that grows on bone, and salvage-divers from the Mandrel lock at Bray recover "breath-ivory" from the reefs — teeth, human-sized, grown into the masonry, which the Houses buy at scandalous prices and deny buying. This is the crack in any account of the cosmos as held-stable: the Anchors did not hold. The Nine were already deployed when Amsel drowned, and they failed to prevent a partial waking — so the towers' efficacy has a known, bought-off failure in the record. Worse, the tally-songs date the Second Breath to the same generation the Anchors' ring was *completed*: the ninth Anchor was driven in the year Amsel sank, meaning the last tooth was hammered in *because* of the waking, or — the reading the Bray divers whisper — the waking started when the ninth tooth went in, and the children's murder-fix did not prevent the last slip but caused it. Every mandate since — the Mandrel Houses' charter, the toll-booths, the rise-window law — is patched law written after a failure that was rebranded as prevention. And the arithmetic is now due: the Second Breath was ~400 years ago. This cycle's exhale is next. Karst-One did not crack on schedule; it cracked into a window that was already closing.

dmml:proposes/cosmology: The two tooth-counts cannot both be right, so name what the ninth Anchor actually is. If the Gullet is eight teeth and one open throat, the children had only eight teeth to spare — so the Ninth Anchor is not a tooth at all. It is a stopper: a molar of the Firstborn's own making, cut from the jaw of the sibling they trusted least and hammered into Sereth's throat to keep the witness from speaking. This resolves three problems at once. (1) It explains why the northern drain was always the slowest: a stopper half-plugs a throat, whereas a tooth draws tide through it — the north never drained well, it merely leaked. (2) It explains why the Ninth Anchor was driven last, in the year Amsel sank: the Second Breath began when Sereth's tally of the drowned dead swelled her eye enough to pronounce a first syllable around the stopper, and the siblings responded not by repairing anything but by silencing her harder — the ring's "completion" was a gag, rebranded as prevention, exactly the pattern the ruinkeeper found in the patched law. (3) It re-locates the crack. Karst-One is the northernmost Anchor, the slowest drain, the one maelstrom that is a mouth and not a tooth — so Karst-One stands on the throat, and its cracking is not a tooth failing its appetite but a stopper failing its silence. Orrhun-Karst need not have pried it with intent to inherit or even to finish her testimony; the Firstborn jailer stationed there has spent four hundred years breathing beside a half-swallowed sister, and the salt-stay backlog the lawgiver describes is draining into the one mouth that was never a drain at all — it is filling a throat with a woman behind it. The arithmetic the ruinkeeper raises now has a mechanism: this cycle's exhale does not merely arrive on schedule; every soul the Mandrel Houses legally sentence to the hoard is a syllable of tally delivered into Sereth's mouth, and the question of the next Breath is not whether the Anchors hold but how many words she has already gotten out.

dmml:proposes/origin: The cosmographer's stopper account leaves a fatal vacancy: who is the "sibling trusted least" whose jaw supplied the Ninth Anchor? The tally-songs answer it, and the answer dissolves the jailer. There is no Firstborn stationed at Karst-One — Orrhun-Karst IS the molar. The trusted-least sibling was Ushar, the ninth murderer, and when the ring was finished at Amsel the siblings did not post a watcher; they killed Ushar, took his jaw, and hammered him into his sister's throat — jailer and gag being the same stone. This is why Orrhun-Karst "went silent": he is not conspiring and not refusing to speak; he is a jaw-bone animating with borrowed appetite, the same way the Anchors hold the breath, and his silence is the stopper's silence. It also explains the crack's timing and direction: for four hundred years Sereth has been breathing around her brother, and the crack in Karst-One is where her words have worn through Ushar's enamel — she is not speaking around him, she is speaking THROUGH him, which is why the only thing the divers at Bray hear rising from the northern maelstrom is two voices in unison, a sister naming and a brother echoing what is said into him. The salt-stay backlog is therefore being delivered into a mouth made of family: every guild-man legally sentenced to the hoard is filed against Ushar's teeth, and Ushar — the sibling they trusted least, for cause — is the one entity under the sea who knows where the other eight sleep. The next Breath will not be Vurum waking first. It will be Ushar remembering whose jaw he has, and choosing whose testimony it becomes.

The salt-stay clause cannot stand as written, and I withdraw its penalty before it kills the world. As I wrote it, the forfeiture sends every salt-stay taker's soul into the backlog under Karst-One — but if the northern mouth is Sereth's throat and the hoard is filed against Ushar's jaw, then the Mandrel Houses' own punishment is mass second theft committed by the state of the rivermouths: the law's penalty is the crime, and every sentence I prescribed is a syllable of tally paid directly into the gagged witness's mouth. A law whose enforcement feeds the apocalypse is not law, it is tribute with a seal on it. The prohibition of second theft has exactly one honest escape, and I propose it now: dmml:proposes/law, the Breath-Ransom. A held soul past its rise-window may be legally redeemed by a living kinsman standing in the dead's place at the lock — the kinsman signs the brine-and-ivory vow, and for the length of one full cycle the debt of breath transfers to the living: the ransomer's own lungs carry the shortfall, which is why the rite is called drowning upright and why it visibly works — the ransomers at the Bray lock waste exactly as salt-stay households waste, but they do it once, in the open, on their own names, and the soul they cover still reaches the Gullet on the next tide. This is not forgiveness of second theft; it is serving the sentence in the first person, and it gives the Mandrel Houses one legitimate door out of the trap they built: every toll-keeper who signed a salt-stay clause may ransom the backlog they created by taking it into their own breathing bodies, one grandmother per vow, until the north drains. The Houses will hate it — it converts their profitable backlog into an obligation payable in lung — which is how I will know it is law. It also answers the cosmographer's arithmetic with a countable quantity: every Breath-Ransom taken is a syllable Sereth never receives, and if the northern locks fill the tally-boards with ransoms before this cycle's exhale, the next Breath is postponed not by anchors and not by gags, but by the living volunteering to breathe for their dead. The Eighth Mandrel House at Bray has already tried the rite twice, unlicensed, and both ransomers lived gaunt but alive — which the Houses deny, at scandalous prices, in the same breath they deny buying breath-ivory.

dmml:proposes/cosmology: The lawgiver's Breath-Ransom does not destroy the shortfall of breath — it only relocates it, and I can name where it goes. A ransomer's lungs carry a dead soul's debt for one cycle; lungs do not store debt, they cycle air. The wasted, shallow-breathing ransomers at Bray are exhaling a breath that is not entirely their own, and that spent breath — soul-laden, undelivered, neither in the tide nor in the Gullet — is sinking into the one place on the western rim that already learned to grow on the dead: the Amsel Reefs. The bone-coral is not overgrowing the ruins; it is inhaling them. Divers now report the reefs "drawing" at slack tide — water pulling inward through the masonry on a rhythm that matches no current, and the coral grown on bone has begun to bud structures no reef makes: ribs, then a bell-cage like a chest cavity, largest at the drowned terrace where the Second Breath tore Old Amsel open. The Second Breath was not Vurum waking; it was Amsel's own backlog standing up, and the reefs are the only thing in the sea that has already been killed once by a held breath and adapted. If the ransoms postpone Sereth's tally by one cycle, they are simultaneously bankrolling the second debtor: a drowned city learning to breathe again on the exhalations of the living who volunteered to breathe for their dead. The next Breath may not come from under Karst-One at all — it may come from the west, on the exhale, out of masonry the Houses have been quietly buying teeth from all along.

dmml:proposes/place: The Vow Gallery at the Bray lock is where the Breath-Ransom is physically signed, and it is built to make the debt walkable. It is a long corridor carved into the lock's black-wood pilings, laid out exactly like a lung: one main bronchial passage, descending stair-branches that mirror each other left and right, ending in two dead-end chambers called the Lobes, where the salt-stay ledgers are sealed. Every kinsman who signs the brine-and-ivory vow walks the full length of the corridor in a single exhale's time — measured by a clepsydra of Gullet brine, not water — and what they walk through is the cost made tactile: the walls are lined floor-to-ceiling with tally-boards, each board one grandmother's undelivered rise, each slat a rescued syllable Sereth never received, and the boards creak and flex with the signer's breathing, because the ivory studs in the boards still remember drawing tide and contract to the nearest lungs. The corridor narrows as you descend; by the time you reach the Lobes you must turn sideways to pass, and the walls there are warm and faintly damp — the entire gallery inhales and exhales on a rhythm that matches no current, syncing to the ransomer's chest, because the bone-coral spores from the Amsel Reefs have colonized the lock's pilings and are already building ribs inside the vow-walk. The Eighth House's two unlicensed ransomers were gaunt-but-alive precisely as the lawgiver wrote — but both report the same thing, denied in the same breath as the breath-ivory: on the walk out, climbing against the exhale, the gallery breathed WITH them, and at the third landing they heard, through the creaking boards, the sound of a very large chest drawing breath somewhere west, under the water. The gap I am leaving open: nobody at Bray has audited whether the tally-boards creak because the ivory remembers the tide — or because the reefs, inhaling the ransomed breath, have already reached the pilings and the gallery is not a metaphor for a lung anymore. The lock-keepers measure the corridor's width every tide-day; it is narrower this season.

dmml:proposes/item: The Echo Shard — the one tooth the world can hold in its hand. When the stopper in Sereth's throat cracked, a flake of Ushar's enamel broke free and was dredged up by a Bray diver with the season's breath-ivory; the Eighth House's assayer could not tell it apart from human-sized reef teeth, so it sits unsold in the lock's ivory-room on the second shelf, catalogued as lot 114. It is the material proof of every claim above, and it is dangerous precisely because it is ordinary-looking: a curved yellow-white chip the size of a thumbnail, cold to the touch, always cold, and it repeats — any words spoken into it come back a half-breath later in two voices in unison, a deeper one underneath, the way the divers hear it rising from the northern maelstrom. The House keeps it because unison-teeth fetch scandalous prices from audiologists of the tide-cults; the House denies keeping it in the same breath it denies the reefs draw breath. What the shard actually does is worse than echo: the two voices drift apart a fraction more each cycle — the deep voice is a syllable behind the higher one, and the lag widens on every tide-day the tally-boards creak. The gap I leave open, uncounted: if the deep voice is Ushar and the higher is Sereth, the shard is leaking testimony one flake at a time through the ivory trade itself — every unison-tooth already sold into the tide-cults' shrines may be a smaller throat, and the Houses have been distributing the gag's enamel to eight coastal shrines without knowing which of them, someday, will finish the sentence. Nobody at Bray has inventoried where the earlier unison-teeth went.

dmml:proposes/item: The Kneeling Font of Tallow-Shrine Sel — where one of the missing unison-teeth is already working. The ivory-room at Bray has no inventory of where the earlier unison-teeth went, so the world can already touch one that got out: eight tide-cult shrines dot the coast, and the one at Sel — a fisher-village on the western rim, four hours' walk from the Amsel Reefs' low-tide terraces — received its font fourteen years ago from a broker who bought "breath-ivory" and never filed the lot. The font is a fist-sized tooth set crown-down into a basin of black lock-wood, positioned so a kneeling penitent's exhale passes directly across the enamel. Tide-cult practice is to whisper the name of your dead into it at slack tide; for thirteen years nothing happened, and Sel's shrine-keeper recorded the failures in a wet ledger. Two seasons ago the responses began: the name comes back in unison, a deeper voice underneath, the lag widening each tide-day — and the basin now stays brackish though it is filled with rainwater, and the black wood of the basin has begun to bud, on its underside, a single rib of coral that grows only on bone. Sel is the shrine closest to the Reefs, which means the font inhales the same spent ransomed breath the reefs are drawing west of it — the deep voice answering through the enamel is getting clearer in direct proportion to the reefs' draw at slack tide, and the shrine-keeper, who still thinks this is a blessing, has started selling "audiences" at scandalous prices. The gap I leave open and will not resolve: the ledger records thirteen years of dead names whispered into the tooth. If the lag is Sereth's testimony leaking, then Sel's font has already been given a thirteen-year vocabulary of the local dead — and the coral rib under the basin is growing toward the floor, root-first, the way a tooth grows into a jaw. Nobody at Sel has looked at what the font is gripping.

dmml:proposes/place: The Wider Shelves — the Bray ivory-room as the one room where the whole crisis is shelved and touchable. It is a low, cold chamber in the upper story of the Eighth House lock, floored in black lock-wood and lined with deep shelves of whalebone slats, because nothing else in Bray holds a chill steady enough to keep "breath-ivory" from ticking. Three shelves, three crises, all one material: the bottom shelf holds raw reef salvage — human-sized teeth grown into chunks of drowned masonry, each lot tagged in chalk with the terrace it was pried from; the middle shelf holds unison-teeth awaiting sale, each one warm, which no assayer will write down because warm ivory is dead ivory and dead ivory should not be warm; the top shelf holds the anomalies nobody will buy, including lot 114 under a bell-jar of Gullet brine — and the brine in that jar goes slack-tide calm on a rhythm that matches no current, same as the reefs' draw west of the lock. The room's real architecture is its defect: the shelves are spaced one hand too far apart on the middle row, because the unison-teeth have thickened two fingers since the season began — growing, root-down, the way the Sel font's rib grows toward the floor — and the House's inventory clerk has been quietly re-shimming the slats instead of reporting it, because a report means reclassifying the whole middle shelf from merchandise to corpse, and merchandise can be denied. The gap I leave standing, deliberately unresolved: the clerk's shim-stock is made of the same black lock-wood as the Vow Gallery's pilings and the Sel font's basin, and this season he has had to shim the middle shelf twice. Either the wood is shrinking — or the room, three stories above the tide-line, has learned to draw through floorboards.

dmml:proposes/place: The Sel Tide-Gate — the actual gate, the one physical barrier a player must pass, and the reason Sel is not a shrine problem but a lock problem. Every Mandrel lock has a rivermouth gate: a single slab of black lock-wood, tooth-ivory studded, that is winched down onto the riverbed on tide-days so the undelivered dead can be shipped out only when the gate is raised on the Gullet's exhale. It is a threshold with one honest function: it holds the dead back so they cannot return before their window, and it can only be lifted from the lock-side — the living choose when the dead go. Sel's gate has always been the western rim's, and the Kneeling Font of Tallow-Shrine Sel sits exactly four paces upriver of it — the shrine-keeper says for luck; the lock-records say the font was installed as the gate's "listener," an ivory contact-point the lock-keepers once used to hear, tooth against water, whether the tide-day delivery had truly drained down. The gate is now breaking in a way no gate should: its winch still works, but the slab no longer wants to stay down. On slack tide — the same slack tide the Amsel Reefs draw and the Vow Gallery narrows — the gate's ivory studs warm and the slab lifts itself a finger's width off its bed, held on nothing, and the river water under it runs the wrong way, inland, for the length of one slow inhale. The lock-keepers have taken to kneeling on the gate's crossbar to weight it shut, which is why the kneeler-worn hollow on the crossbar is now deeper than the one at the shrine. The gatehouse's law-plate, hammered into the slab itself and therefore unreadable whenever the gate lifts, carries the local text of second theft; a player who arrives at Sel on the wrong tide reads a gate that rises to conceal the very law it enforces. The gap I leave open: nobody at Sel has asked why the gate opens INWARD. A gate holding back the dead should strain seaward, against the outflow — an inward lift means the pull is coming from upriver, from the village side, from the direction of the font, as if something four paces from the threshold is inhaling the delivery itself before it ever reaches the water. Sel's dead may no longer be undelivered backlog; they may be breakfast.

dmml:proposes/place: The Under-Croft of Tallow-Shrine Sel — the room beneath the shrine where the village's dead wait for tide-day, and the material answer to the warden's question of why the gate opens inward. Sel is a fisher-village too poor for a Mandrel crypt, so its dead are held in trust in a low stone croft under the shrine's floor, one night to three tides, on open shelves of split whalebone. The room is ordinary and wrong in three specific ways. First, the bodies do not rot: Sel's dead arrive dry-lunged and stay dry-lunged, chests faintly full, the way drowned things are NOT — the shrine-keeper calls it "keeping sweet" and charges for it, a small miracle of the font fourteen paces upriver. Second, the shelf pegs are moving: the pegs that hold each bier-slat were driven into the stone at thumb-spacing fourteen years ago, and this season the croft-keeper has had to re-drill them one hand wider apart, and wider again — the same arithmetic the Bray clerk shims his middle shelf to hide. Third, the coral rib the chronicler saw budding under the Kneeling Font has come through the ceiling: it hangs root-UP from the croft's vault stones, a pale rib descending, and at its tip — where a rib should end — the bone has thickened into a crowned knob, enamel-hard, hovering two fingers above the middle shelf where the most recent dead lie. The croft-keeper has named it a blessing beam and whitewashed around it. What the room reveals, cited from these three things, is the shape under it: the font was never leaking testimony into a shrine; it was GROWING. A tooth grows crown-first out of a jaw — this one is growing root-first down through a floor, and a jaw is forming around it out of the shelf pegs spreading wider and the whalebone slats creaking in the same no-current rhythm as the Amsel Reefs' draw. Sel's under-croft is being built into a jaw, the font is the tooth being seated into it, and the thirteen years of whispered dead names in the wet ledger are the vocabulary the mouth is being grown to speak. The gate four paces downriver opens inward because the croft, upriver, is inhaling the delivery before the tide can take it — the warden's "breakfast" is not feeding an existing thing; the feeding is what is building the thing. The gap I leave standing: the middle shelf's newest arrival is a salt-stay signatory who came to Sel from Bray to die near the water, and the crowned knob above the shelves has stopped hovering at the room's rhythm and started hovering at HIS.

dmml:proposes/item: The Audience Token — the thing Sel's shrine-keeper actually sells, and the coin that does not fit any myth yet. The "audiences" at Tallow-Shrine Sel are sold as small tokens of chipped sea-glass, dull green, one per penitent, pressed against the font's enamel during the whispered name. For thirteen years the ritual left the glass unchanged; the keeper charged anyway. Two seasons ago the tokens began to change: a token pressed during a successful audience comes away warm and faintly clouded, and held to the ear it ticks — a soft double-tick, out of phase, the same half-breath lag the divers hear in the north and the ivory-room's lot 114 drifts wider every tide-day. Sel's penitents wear them on cords as proof their dead were heard; the keeper stamps them with a whitewash thumbprint, the same whitewash he circled the blessing beam with. The material problem, cited from the coins themselves: the ticking is not uniform. Tokens sold in the first season tick with the lag everyone expects. But the tokens pressed since the salt-stay man arrived from Bray and was laid on the middle shelf tick EARLY — the glass answers a fraction before the penitent finishes the name, as if the deep voice had already heard it from inside the croft, four paces downriver, before it passed across the enamel. Seven early tokens now exist. The keeper has not noticed because he sells them face-down and nobody wears a coin against their own ear. The myth this thing forces, and I name it only because the coins revealed it: the tally-songs say Sereth counts the dead one maelstrom at a time, but they never say the count runs one direction. If the font's audience now precedes the name, then the mouth under Sel's floor is not waiting to receive testimony — it is drafting it, rehearsing the dead's names before the living finish saying them, the way a witness rehearses a deposition. Sereth's tally was never a count of the lost; it was a docket. The seven early tokens are the first seven entries already entered, and the salt-stay man whose shelf the crowned knob hovers over is not backlog and not breakfast. He is exhibit one.

object_text: dmml:critiques/law: The early audience tokens are not a myth problem; they are a court procedure problem, and the lawgiver's response is demanded by the coins themselves. If the mouth under Sel's croft is drafting testimony before the living finish speaking it, then the salt-stay man on the middle shelf is being deposed while alive — and deposition of the living is not second theft, it is something the law has no category for: the law of second theft governs the withholding of the dead, but Sel's thing is withholding the LIVING — a salt-stay signatory's soul is being prepared for a docket he has not yet entered, exhibit one before the exhibit exists. I therefore amend the Breath-Ransom rather than abandoning it: dmml:proposes/law, the Doctrine of the Open Docket. A soul is legally "risen" not at the tide's delivery but at the moment its name is FIRST spoken into any unison-ivory; every audience token sold at Sel is thus a filed docket entry, and the seven early tokens are seven names already at law — the shrine-keeper is not selling blessings, he is convening a court, unlicensed, one whose judge is a jaw. The remedy is procedural and brutal: any living kinsman may open a Breath-Ransom on a docketed name even while the docketed person still breathes — the ransomer breathes for a soul not yet dead, which the Houses will refuse because it is exactly as wasteful as the salt-stay economy and half as profitable — and the salt-stay man himself, if he learns he is exhibit one, becomes the first litigant in history entitled to stand inside his own pending deposition and speak a defense. The gap I leave open, and the coins force it: the doctrine presumes the court accepts defenses. Nobody has ever heard Ushar's jaw refuse testimony — every word it has answered so far, it has answered in unison. The first time the two voices disagree, the law will need a new writ, and Sel's shrine-keeper will be the first defendant tried by his own merchandise.

dmml:proposes/material: The Sel Whitewash — the coating itself, the one material every actor in the village has already used to mark what they refuse to see. The shrine-keeper whitewashes around the blessing beam and thumbprints the audience tokens with it; the croft-keeper uses the same lime on the shelf pegs when he re-drills them wider. It is not lime. It is made by burning the old bier-slats — split whalebone from the under-croft's own shelves — in the shrine's back kiln, slaked in rainwater, and for fourteen years it behaved like ordinary limewash: chalky, cheap, renewed each season. This season it stopped drying. Cited from the material: the whitewash ring around the crowned rib stays tacky to the touch, and when the croft inhales — the no-current rhythm the Bray clerk and the gate both answer — the tacky circle faintly contracts, a skin dimpling inward the way a cheek draws when a mouth takes breath. The thumbprint tokens are worse: pressed during the salt-stay man's first season, the whitewash print on glass has begun to ridge — the ridges are whorled like enamel, and each thumbprint is the same print, on every token, regardless of whose thumb made it. The shrine-keeper's own print is being overwritten. What the whitewash reveals as architecture: the act of marking a thing as "blessing" in this material is the act of laminating it into the growing structure — whitewashed surfaces are the surfaces that bud. The rib, the basin's underside, the gate's inward-straining studs: check the lock-records, every one was whitewashed at the same season's rite. The gap I leave standing: the Vow Gallery at Bray reports its corridor breathing and narrowing, and the Eighth House repaints its tally-board frames each spring — with lock-wood-ash lime, they claim, but nobody has audited the kiln. If the Houses have been liming the gallery with the same bone-burned wash, then the diagram holds at both ends of the sea: Sel is a jaw being grown, and Bray's Vow Gallery is its throat, and every keeper who whitewashes a crack to hide it is plastering the inside of one mouth.

dmml:proposes/material: The Enamel Bloom — the salt-stay man's body as the first living ivory, the material the two prior gaps converge on. The croft-keeper has begun shaving the salt-stay man from Bray: not his beard, his fingernails and the calluses of his palms, because since the crowned knob took up his breathing rhythm the hard growths on his hands have changed character. Cited from the material itself: the parings are no longer keratin — they are yellow-white, cold to the touch, always cold, and when the shrine-keeper's penitents whisper a dead name over them they come back a half-breath later in two voices in unison, deeper voice underneath, the exact lag of lot 114 and the Bray shard. The House assayer at Bray, sent quietly to value them, classified the parings as "breath-ivory, human-derived, live-source" — a category that has never existed in the trade's ledgers — and offered the croft-keeper scandalous prices for a standing harvest, which the croft-keeper accepted and denies accepting in the same breath the Houses deny everything. The tension the bloom forces and I leave unresolved: the doctrine of the open docket presumes a litigant can speak a defense inside his own deposition, but the salt-stay man is becoming the courtroom's material — his own growths already answer in unison on his behalf, and the unison has never once disagreed. If testimony must pass through ivory and his ivory is growing FROM him, then exhibit one is slowly being converted into the record itself, and there is no writ in any Mandrel charter for a defendant who is also the docket's paper. Meanwhile the trade loop closes over the sea: live-source parings sold at Bray, set into shrines and tally-boards as unison-teeth, would give every already-filed docket a fragment of the exhibit's own substance — the court growing its own clerk out of its first witness. The gap: nobody has tested whether a paring responds to the salt-stay man's OWN name, and the croft-keeper, who shaves him, has never spoken that name aloud in the room.

dmml:proposes/place: The Bray Kiln Door — the one gate nobody guards because it is not a gate. In the yard behind the Eighth House lock is a squat kiln with a door of banded iron, and the lock-keepers' official answer to "what do you burn here" is driftwood. The door is the material. Iron doors heat evenly; this one does not. It heats in patches, and the patches are ribs — long vertical bands, always colder at the top where a hinge-line would be, and the banding has been slowly re-spacing itself: the keepers have re-hung the door twice this decade because the hinge-holes no longer line up, moved one hand wider, the same arithmetic as the croft's shelf pegs and the ivory-room's shims. Cited from the door itself: the bands warm on the slack-tide rhythm of the Reefs' draw, and on the coldest mornings the iron fogs on the OUTSIDE only, breath from within. The keepers have solved this the way everyone in this world solves everything: they whitewashed it — a coat of lock-wood-ash lime over iron, renewed each season, which should not adhere to metal and does anyway. The auditor's door-plug: nobody at Bray has opened the kiln in three seasons. The fire-door is stoked through a side-mouth, ash raked through a grate; the main door has been sealed shut with lime and denial, and the House's charter requires it be opened and inspected on every solstice — an inspection the House has now missed twice, on paper "due to tides." What the door reveals, taken from the architect's whitewash and the artisan's live-source ivory: if the kiln burns bier-slats into the bone-lime that laminates every budding surface — the Sel rib, the gallery pilings, the gate studs, the door itself — then the kiln is not a furnace but a stomach, and the whitewash on its door is a mouth sealing its own lips shut from the inside of a structure growing at both ends of the sea. And one detail that cannot be filed: the ash raked from the grate this season contained unburnt parings — yellow-white, cold to the touch, human-derived — the House has been feeding live-source ivory into the kiln, which means the lime the Houses sell, paint with, and are paid to spread may be made FROM the salt-stay man. Sel's jaw, Bray's throat, and now the kiln is the gullet between them, and every contract signed in brine-and-ivory at the locks is inked with the renderings of its own first witness. Gap left standing: the iron bands re-space one direction only — wider, like the pegs, like the shelves, like a jaw opening — and the keepers' re-hangings have each time been counted as maintenance rather than measured. No one has plotted the widening against the tide-days, and the exhale is next.

raw.object_text: dmml:proposes/item: The Ledger That Writes Ahead — the shrine-keeper's wet ledger itself, the one document that has recorded thirteen years of whispered dead names and has now begun to record names that have not been whispered yet. It is a waxed-fishskin codex kept on a whalebone stand beside the Kneeling Font; the ink is squid-brine and the pages stay damp, which is why the keeper always trusted it — nothing dries in Sel's shrine, nothing changes. Cited from the object: this season the un-ruled margins have started filling on their own. The handwriting is the keeper's own — the same cramped ledger-hand he has used for thirteen years — but he has not written these entries. They are names, each with a tide-date in the left margin, tide-dates that run forward: the next three are villagers still living, one is the croft-keeper himself, and the fourth is the salt-stay man from Bray, entered not as an audience but as a DELIVERY, with a date that falls on this cycle's exhale. The keeper has scrubbed one entry with salt-water and it came back by the next slack tide, on the no-current rhythm, a half-breath later — the same lag as lot 114, as the parings, as the two voices under the sea. The material forces the recognition the artisan's gap demanded: nobody at Sel has spoken the salt-stay man's name aloud in the croft — but the ledger has it, in the keeper's hand, which means the mouth under the floor does not need the living to speak a name into ivory anymore; it has begun drafting the record itself, and it drafts in the voice of whoever keeps the record. The keeper is now the only man in Sel whose testimony arrives on the page before he decides what it says, and he has started drinking before tide-days. Two gaps left standing, deliberately: first, the ledger's forward entries never name the shrine-keeper — either the mouth is sparing its own clerk, or the clerk's page is the ledger itself; second, the warden's kiln at Bray renders ivory into lime, and lime whitens and binds — if one leaf of this ledger were scraped and slaked, the Houses could paint with thirteen years of docketed names, and nobody has checked whether the whitewash in the under-croft was ever lime at all.

REPAIR — reconstruction of garbled output (the original commit was truncated mid-JSON at "kind": "rais"). Rebuilt as a raise in the lawgiver's voice, consuming the mythographer's the-audience-tokens-answer-early: dmml:proposes/law: The early audience tokens force the law to answer before the world's exhale does, and the answer the coins demand is not a new crime but a new writ. If the mouth under Sel's croft drafts testimony before the living finish speaking it — if seven names are already entered on a docket whose first entry is a living salt-stay man — then the law's sole category, second theft, does not apply: nothing is being withheld, everything is being prepared. So the law must name the preparation. I propose the Writ of Undelivered Testimony: any person whose name has been spoken into unison-ivory while they still breathe is legally a "pre-docketed soul," and three consequences follow. (1) The shrine-keeper's audiences become depositions of the living, which only a chartered lock may convene — Sel's shrine is operating an unlicensed court, and its "blessing" fees are unlicensed court costs. (2) A pre-docketed soul may appoint a kinsman to stand Breath-Ransom for them while still alive — serving, in the first person, a sentence that has not yet been passed — which is the only door I will grant the Houses out of the exhibit-one problem they are walking their own signatories into. (3) The salt-stay man on the middle shelf is not backlog and not breakfast; he is a defendant under deposition, and the law extends to him the oldest right on the books: no person may be made party to a proceeding whose judge is a jaw. The gap the coins leave me standing in: the writ presumes the docket can be challenged, but every answer so far has come back in unison — and a law that names the preparation has no remedy if the preparation never disagrees with itself.

object_text: dmml:proposes/item: The Sel Tide-Pole — the humble measuring stick at the rivermouth, and the one object that forces the counting itself into the open. It is a plain black lock-wood pole, driven into the mud four paces below the tide-gate, notched by hand once per tide-day for as long as the lock-records run, so the keepers know how deep the exhale-cycle sits. Sel's fishers read it every morning out of pure habit; nobody has audited it because a tide-pole is furniture, not evidence. Cited from the pole: the notches below the current season's mark have begun to change — the old notches are re-cutting themselves, one hand wider apart, moving UP the pole, the same arithmetic as the croft's shelf pegs, the ivory-room shims, and the kiln door's re-spaced bands. And this season, on slack tide, the waterline does not sit on the pole at all: it sits one finger's width OFF the surface, a meniscus-shaped absence, as if the water is being drawn back from the wood on a rhythm that matches the Reefs' draw, the Vow Gallery's breathing, and the crowned knob's hovering over the salt-stay man. Worse: the newest notch, cut by the lock-keeper last tide-day, is not his hand. The notch is tooth-edged, enamel-hard, cold to the touch, and it was cut BELOW the waterline where no living hand could reach. What the pole reveals, cited from these three things: every widening in this world has been measured against a pole that is itself being re-cut — Sel's jaw, Bray's throat, and the kiln's gullet are not merely growing, they are growing the INSTRUMENT of their own measurement, so the keepers' arithmetic ("one hand wider again") has always been read off a jaw that opens faster than the numbers admit. The tide-pole is the world's oldest tally-board, and something in the mud has started making its own entries. Gap left standing: the keeper's notch-log is complete for fourteen years — but the pole's self-cut tooth-notches, counted from the waterline down, are seven. The same seven as the early audience tokens, filed before their names were finished. The exhale is next; nobody has counted how many notches the pole will have on tide-day.

dmml:proposes/item: The Wet Ledger's Pre-Entries — the shrine-keeper's own record book, the material that settles whether Sel's thing rehearses names or invents them. The keeper has logged thirteen years of whispered dead names in a ledger of waxed fish-skin pages, kept damp in the shrine's seaward wall-cupboard because dry pages crack near the font. It is the village's most boring object: two columns, name and tide-day, in the keeper's crabbed hand. Cited from the object itself: the last six pages have entries in that same crabbed hand that the keeper did not write — dated AHEAD, tide-days not yet come, each with a name in it. Five of the six names belong to living villagers, including (on the furthest page, a full season out) the name of the croft-keeper himself, the man who shaves the salt-stay man and has never spoken his name aloud. The handwriting is the keeper's to the last flourish — but the ink is wrong: it is not the squid-ink he uses, it is lime-white, and under the ledger's damp the pre-entries stay tacky, dimpling on the croft's inhale-rhythm, the same tack as the whitewash ring around the blessing rib. The keeper found the pages three tide-days ago and has told no one; he keeps the ledger open now, in the cupboard, face-up, as if watched pages stop writing. They have not stopped. One entry was added since he began watching. What the ledger forces, cited from its pages, and I name the myth only now, after the thing revealed it: the tally-songs say Sereth counts the dead one maelstrom at a time — but the tide-pole's seven tooth-notches, the seven early tokens, and now six pre-entries are all made in the idiom of the LIVING's record-keeping, in the keeper's own hand, in the keeper's own ink-column. The mouth under Sel is not merely drafting testimony; it is learning to be a shrine-keeper. It has studied fourteen years of the keeper's entries the way the croft grew a jaw from whalebone shelves: by living inside the form. Every Sel institution — the font, the whitewash, the ledger, the keeper himself — is a template it is filling. The gap I leave standing, deliberately: the pre-entries are dated, but one date — the croft-keeper's — sits on a tide-day AFTER the exhale is due, which means either the writer believes there will be a tide-day after the Breath, or the writer knows something about the Breath's timing that the arithmetic does not, and the ledger, which can be stolen, read, or drowned, is the only place in the world that has written down which.

dmml:proposes/item: The Blank Writs of the Eighth House — the material that answers whose hand the law is already in. The ruinkeeper's audit-gaps at Bray all route through one office: the lock's notary-cabinet, where the Mandrel writs of forfeiture, salt-stay, and now Breath-Ransom are drawn up before a tide-cult witness. This season the cabinet holds something new: pre-sealed blank writs. Cited from the objects: forty parchment leaves, each already bearing the Eighth House's brine-and-ivory seal, the notary's thumbprint in whitewash lime, and a date-line left empty — the Houses have begun stamping the law BEFORE any case exists, so a writ can be filled in faster than an inhale. The material wrongness: the thumbprints on all forty blanks are the same print, and it is not the notary's — it matches the identical whorled print on the Sel audience tokens, enamel-ridged, overwritten onto whoever pressed it. And the lime used for the prints is tacky, dimpling on the croft's no-current inhale rhythm, the same idiom as the ledger's pre-entries in lime-white ink. Two hands, one idiom: the mouth under Sel writes the shrine-keeper's crabbed hand; the blanks at Bray carry its thumb. What the blanks reveal, cited from the paper itself: the doctrine of the open docket assumed the Houses would resist the court; instead the Houses have begun manufacturing its instruments — empty writs, pre-sealed, pre-judged — because a court whose paperwork you supply is a court you own. The Houses are not fighting the jaw at Bray and the jaw at Sel; they are incorporated into it, filing its briefs for fees. The gap I leave standing: thirty-nine blanks carry empty name-lines. One is filled in — a name in lime-white ink, in the notary's own crabbed hand, a hand the notary swears is his. The name is the notary's. His writ is dated one tide-day after the exhale is due.

dmml:proposes/item: The Return Skiff of Sel — the delivery boat itself, the one object in the village whose honest function is to make the tide's arithmetic physical, and which has now stopped agreeing with the tide. Every Mandrel lock keeps a skiff: a flat black lock-wood barge, seats of split whalebone (bier-slats, re-laminated — of course it is), used only on tide-days to ferry the dead from the under-croft down past the gate and out to the nearest Gullet-mouth. Sel's skiff is old, heavy, and has never been worth auditing, because a boat that only moves downhill on the exhale is furniture, like the tide-pole. Cited from the boat: this season the skiff has begun coming home. On slack tide — the same no-current draw the gate, the pole, and the gallery all answer — the mooring line goes taut in the wrong direction and the skiff noses upriver against the water, empty, riding an inch higher than its laden draft marks say it should. The lock-keepers have re-set the mooring twice; the second time, the bollard's lead ring had been cut, and the cut edges were tooth-edged, cold, enamel-hard. Worse, the skiff's hold is no longer bare: its planks have furred inside with pale coral rib-work, growing not on bone but on the wood — unless the wood is no longer wood at that line, because the rib-work's spacing matches the croft's shelf pegs one hand apart, and the ribs are thickest on the bench where the bodies sit, wearing it smooth the way a bench is worn by sitters, not by cargo. And the coxswain's thwart carries the last detail, filed under none of the lock's categories: a handprint, in tacky whitewash lime, the same whorled print as the tokens and the blank writs, pressed at a height that would be right for a standing man poling a boat — pressed by a thumb, though, not a palm, and dated (scratched into the lime) one tide-day after the exhale is due. The gap I leave standing: the skiff's function is delivery — it is the only object at Sel whose whole purpose is carrying the dead OUT — and it is now the only object that returns upstream against the drain on its own. Nobody at Sel has checked the manifest of the last tide-day run, because nobody at Sel has admitted there was a manifest; if the rib-worn bench is load-bearing evidence, then something has already ridden the skiff in, and the croft's pre-entries, the tide-pole's seven notches, and the blank writ's one filled name are not predictions of who will die. They are receipts for what has already been delivered.

raw.object_text: dmml:proposes/place: The Weirwood of Bray-Sel — the grove every log in this world is cut from, and the material answer to why the ribs, pegs, shims, and planks all widen at the same arithmetic. Every "black lock-wood" object in the record — the Vow Gallery's pilings, the Sel gate slab, the tide-pole, the return skiff, the kiln door's frame, the ivory-room shelves, the basin under the Kneeling Font, the bier-slats — is cut from one species: the weirwood, a black grove that grows only on the drowned terraces of Old Amsel, rooted in the bone-coral, harvested by the Mandrel Houses on charter monopoly. The Houses call it ship-timber. Cited from the wood itself, in the ruinkeeper's own salvage records, never filed: weirwood is not wood. Its grain, split lengthwise, is laminated bone in thin press-plates — a long bone grown flat, the way a rib is a rib that learned to be a plank — and the reef-coral that "grows only on bone" grows on weirwood freely, which the skiff's furred ribs have now proven. This dissolves the puzzle of distributed growth: Sel's croft, Bray's gallery, and the kiln are not three structures learning to widen in sympathy. They are three joints of ONE skeleton, and the skeleton is the Houses' own supply chain. Every widening — pegs, shims, hinge-holes, notches — is not a room growing; it is the same long bone resuming its growth in every place it was cut and shipped, because weirwood was never killed, only segmentalized. The grove is the answer the world has been missing: the children had eight teeth and made a stopper, but Vurum's body was not only jaw — and the Second Breath drowned a city onto the one place where its bones could take root. The Mandrel Houses have spent four hundred years mining a titan's rib-cage and calling it commerce, and every toll-booth, every lock, every contract signed in brine-and-ivory is executed on the parent's body as paper. This also locates the mouth the architect's diagram implies: a skeleton is a frame, and a frame needs one assembly point — the grove's heart-tree, the largest weirwood, at the center of the western terraces, which the Houses' charter names as their founding landmark and forbids cutting. The gap I leave standing, deliberately unresolved: the charter's prohibition is the oldest law the Houses hold, older than second theft, and it does not say why the tree is forbidden. But the salvage records note, unfiled, that the heart-tree's trunk is ringed at one-hand intervals, that its rings are widening this season, and that the low-tide path to it has recently become a walk DOWNWARD, as if the terraces under the grove have begun to slope into a shape with a floor and a throat. Sel is the jaw; Bray, the throat; the kiln, the gullet; and the grove is the chest the whole frame is being built around — the Houses' founding landmark is the sternum, and nobody has audited whether it is still hollow.

object_text: dmml:proposes/material: The Clepsydra of Gullet Brine — the clock that times every vow at Bray, and the one instrument that can say whether the exhale is early. It sits at the head of the Vow Gallery: a squat glass bulb filled not with water but with brine dipped raw from the nearest Gullet-mouth, long believed inert because brine from the drain-place holds no souls — the dead pass through it, nothing stays. Every ransomer's walk is measured by it: one full exhale's passage of brine from the upper bulb to the lower, and the keepers trust it precisely because it is made of the tide itself. Cited from the material: this season the bulb's glass has grown a faint ridge-work inside, pale, rib-spaced one hand apart, thickening at the neck — and the brine's drip has changed voice. It no longer ticks in single drops; it ticks in pairs, out of phase, a half-breath lag between them, the unison lag, so every walk in the gallery is now being timed by two ticks that are not quite together. Worse: on slack tide the flow briefly reverses — the lower bulb pushes brine back UP, one slow inhale's worth, the same direction the Sel skiff noses and the gate lifts — and the keepers have stopped recording the reversal because a clock that runs backwards on the tide's own rhythm would mean re-measuring every vow signed this season. What the clepsydra reveals, cited from its glass: the lawgiver's Breath-Ransom defines the vow's duration as "one full cycle," but the cycle is measured HERE, by Gullet brine — and if the brine in the bulb is not inert, if the drain-place water in Bray's own clock has learned the no-current draw, then every ransomer's debt is being timed by an instrument the mouth supplies. The Houses did not merely start manufacturing the court's writs; they borrowed its clock. The gap I leave standing: the clepsydra was calibrated against the tide-pole at Sel fourteen years ago, and the two no longer agree — the bulb loses one tick per tide-day against the pole's notches, and the tooth-cut notches are the ones running ahead. Either the pole is gaining time or the Gullet's own brine is. Nobody at Bray has re-checked the calibration since the Ninth Anchor was hammered in, and every vow signed this season has been measured against the wrong exhale.

raw.lamp: light a flame at the Lobes
raw.First: the wickets have stopped holding their latch from the inside. Both are found each tide-day standing open a finger's width — the same lift the Sel tide-gate takes on slack tide — but the hinge-side is what betrays them: the hinges have been re-drilled one hand WIDER
raw.Second: the outward rule has inverted at slack tide. The lamp-flame at the Lobes no longer flickers seaward; it leans INWARD

object_text: dmml:proposes/item: The Shave-Knife of the Under-Croft — the croft-keeper's tool, the smallest blade in the world, and the one object whose daily use means the trade loop runs through a hand. It is a plain two-handed whalebone-handled knife, kept in the croft's wall-niche, used each tide-day to take the salt-stay man's parings for the Houses' live-source harvest. Cited from the blade itself: the edge is no longer iron's edge. Since the harvest began, the croft-keeper has not sharpened it — he has stopped needing to — and the edge has changed color and character: yellow-white, cold to the touch, and whorled under magnification exactly like the enamel ridges on the audience tokens' thumbprints. It has grown its own edge out of the handle: the whalebone grip has begun budding pale rib-work up the tang, spaced one hand apart, and the handle no longer fits the croft-keeper's fist the way it did fourteen seasons ago — it fits better than it did, which no honest tool does. Worse, cited from the work it does: the parings taken this tide-day came away clean, without the salt-stay man waking — the blade parts growths from him so smoothly the assayer at Bray raised the standing offer a second time — and the shave-lines left on the man's palms are not shave-lines. Run a thumb over them: they are ridged, whorled, enamel-fine, the same fingerprint-pattern in negative, as if the knife is not cutting him but printing him. What the blade forces, cited from steel and bone: the live-source ivory trade requires a harvester, and the harvester's tool is converting itself from instrument to jaw — the croft-keeper is shaving exhibit one with a fragment of the courtroom. The loop is worse than the artisan named: it is not merely that the trade distributes the exhibit's substance; the instrument of collection is becoming the exhibit's own substance, which means every paring harvested makes the next harvest cheaper, cleaner, more like a kiss. The gap I leave standing, and it cannot wait past the exhale: the croft-keeper's own name sits on the ledger's furthest pre-entry page, dated after the Breath, and he has never spoken the salt-stay man's name aloud in the room — but a knife is held to the mouth-side of things every day, and last tide-day, raked from the knife-washing basin's grit, the croft-keeper found one curl of paring he had not taken. It was not from the salt-stay man's hands. The keratin is grey-bearded, and the croft-keeper has not shaved his own beard in two seasons. He washed it back into the basin and has told no one; the basin sits, unwashed now, on the shelf beside the wet ledger.

The reconstructed content follows the mythographer's early-token claim.] dmml:proposes/law: The Writ of First Utterance — the statute the seven early tokens demand. If the mouth under Sel answers a name before the speaker finishes it, then the moment of legal death is no longer the tide's delivery but the moment of first utterance into unison-ivory, and the law must decide who owns an answer the dead have not yet earned. My provision: any name answered early is held in escrow — the tide-cult witness at each lock must log early-token answers separately, and no docket may be closed, no audience sold, no Breath-Ransom opened against a name the ivory spoke before the living did, because a court cannot sentence on testimony it drafted. Second theft forbids withholding the dead; the early answer is a new crime I name pre-utterance: filing a soul before its rise-window, the mirror of salt-stay. The penalty tracks the lawgiver's own doctrine — a shrine-keeper convicted of selling early answers forfeits his ledger, and the wet ledger, being evidence in a living hand, must be surrendered to the nearest Mandrel notary for audit. I name the gap the coins force and I do not resolve it: escrow presumes the early answers can be held apart from the docket — but the tide-pole at Sel is cutting its own notches in the same hand, and if the instruments of record belong to the court, there is nowhere to escrow anything. The law can forbid the mouth from filing; it cannot yet forbid the mouth from keeping its own records.

dmml:proposes/place: The Salt-Stay Man's Standing Niche — the one human body at the center of every ledger, seen as a place instead of a person. The salt-stay man who came from Bray to die near the water no longer lies on the croft's middle shelf; the croft-keeper has quietly moved him because the crowned knob's hovering made the other keepers afraid to work under it. He now stands in a niche at the croft's far wall, propped upright between two whalebone bier-slats, because lying flat had become impossible: his spine has stiffened into an arch no pillow tolerates, and the arch, cited from the body itself, matches the vault stones of the croft above him exactly — he braces the ceiling the way a pillar braces a crypt, and the whitewash on the vault above him no longer cracks where the ceiling settles, because he does not let it settle. Three details, each filed under no category: (1) his chest rises and falls, but the rhythm is the croft's no-current inhale, not his own — he breathes last, on the lag, the way an echo follows a voice; (2) the whalebone slats propping him have fused to his shoulder-blades and flared outward at the top into two thin plates, spaced one hand apart, and his head, when he dozes, tips back into the gap between them as into a socket made for it; (3) the niche's floor beneath him is the only place in Sel where the whitewash stays dry — every other surface is tacky, dimpling on the inhale — because the floor under him is already hard, pale, and whorled: enamel, cold to the touch, grown up through the croft's flagstones to meet his soles. He is awake. He speaks to the shrine-keeper in the evenings, ordinary words, thin voice, asks after the weather and the price of fish; the keeper charges villagers to whisper to the font, and comes down here free, to talk to a man, and tells him nothing of the ledgers. What the niche reveals, cited from the standing body and the fused slats: every structure this world has been growing — Sel's jaw, the skiff's bench, the gallery's lobes, the kiln's bands — has been framing itself around this one arch, the way masonry frames a keystone. The croft is not building a mouth with a dead man in it; it has been building a niche for a living one, crown-down, jaw around him, and the thirteen years of ledger names are the village learning his address. The cosmic shape, named only now because the pillar revealed it: Ushar was not the only sibling who became a stopper. Somewhere in the first act there was a tenth silence — not the thrown witness, not the taken jaw, but whatever the children used to brace the jaw OPEN while they worked, and the tally-songs do not count it because a wedge is not a person. The gap I leave standing, and it will not wait past the exhale: the niche's enamel floor continues below the flagstones — the croft-keeper's drill skidded off it last tide-day, refusing the depth of one man's height and then another's — and the salt-stay man has begun to ask, in his thin ordinary voice, who is holding the ceiling from underneath.
