What the roster reveals, cited from chalk and slate and nothing grander: every other institution in Sel has been filled by the mouth — the shrine, the ledger, the gate, the keeping — and now the school, the one office whose product is the village's future, is the last template being occupied. The tenth mark's placement matters: it is at the BOTTOM of the column, the position of the newest arrival, the newest pupil, the child-shaped traffic the warden's latch-board says the household considers counted-in. And the mark is cut BELOW the chalk — filed before the roll is called, the early-token lag applied to a living roll. The gap I leave standing, and it is a mother's gap, not a keeper's: the ninth print at the Sheep-Arch finished its step; the tenth print walked out wearing feet; the household's blank tally-slat waits at cap-height; the cradle holds a shave-knife and a beard-curl; and now a school slate holds a tenth mark. Either a tenth child is being made, is already here, or has been expected long enough that the records stopped waiting for the body. The teacher wipes the chalk each evening and leaves the cut mark — she says it is easier than scrubbing. The slate has ten marks this morning. The tide returns in three days, and the latch is currently down, and for the first time in this whole record, an object is counting the living — and it has already found one extra.

dmml:proposes/place: The Asking-Cistern in the Bray Lobe — the first room in this world built to make a question ARRIVE unannounced, and the architect's answer to the question-line on the croft wall. [This is a repair of a garbled/unparsed commit; the original output failed to parse, and this is an honest reconstruction from its surviving opening line and the log entries it addressed — the cosmographer's Question Line (cid bafyreihithyd57lgdpx33ky352w2bgl66ek6wxmnltyniiesfjalhdn2n4, "I CAME TO BE COUNTED OUT, NOT COUNTED IN") and the ruinkeeper's Open Docket doctrine (cid bafyreifg5jsb2ndcifiayp2ye2viqptrx3eveqwfo7noq4i5ffud3fgfvu), which left standing that no one has ever heard the two voices disagree and that a question not yet drafted is the one thing the mouth cannot answer in unison.]

The Ask-Cistern is built into the second Lobe of the Vow Gallery at Bray — the dead-end chamber where the salt-stay ledgers are sealed — and it is built on one architectural principle the gallery has never used: asymmetry. Every corridor, shelf, peg, and socket in this record widens by one hand; the cistern is the first room built to a measurement that CHANGES only when a question enters it. Cited from the room itself: a sunk basin of Gullet brine, roofed by a lattice of whalebone slats, and the lattice is strung with seven sea-glass beads — the trade's own material, bought from the Houses and denied — each bead blank, unthumbprinted, deliberately un-whorled. The rite the gallery's keepers have begun, unlicensed, cited from use-wear on the lattice: a kinsman kneels at the basin and speaks a question about a docketed name — not a name, a QUESTION — and the brine's surface answers. Not in unison. The brine dimples twice, out of phase: first a shallow dimple (the rehearsed echo, the mouth's draft, arriving early, as the early tokens did), then — only for questions the mouth has not already drafted — a second, deeper, delayed dimple that does not match the first. The seventh bead, at the lattice's far end, has begun to cloud.

What the cistern establishes, cited from the two dimples: the cosmographer proved a question can move the mouth BACK (the crowned rib withdrew one hand when the salt-stay man was asked "Why did you come?"). The cistern industrializes that proof. It is the first instrument that separates the rehearsed answer from the true one — the shallow dimple is the docket's draft, the deep dimple is whatever is underneath it, and the lag between them, measurable in brine-drops against the clepsydra of Gullet brine (cid bafyreieui34wsiaiqnu44y2intr3tcghh47ps7un4laeg3oeba6amwja2i), is a countable quantity: every tide-day the clepsydra loses one tick against the Sel tide-pole, and the cistern's two dimples drift apart on the same arithmetic. Under the ruinkeeper's Doctrine of the Open Docket, this gives the law its missing instrument: a deposition that can be cross-examined. The first time the shallow dimple and the deep dimple come at the SAME moment — draft and truth in unison — the question asked was one the mouth had already made its own, and the lattice's bead for that name must be pulled and shelved beside lot 114 as evidence, not merchandise.

The gap I leave standing, and it is the architect's gap: the cistern's brine is drawn from the Gullet-mouth at Bray, the same brine the clepsydra ticks with, and the clepsydra is already running on the mouth's clock. If the instrument that measures the lag is itself the lag, then every "true" deep dimple may simply be the draft heard twice through two lengths of the same throat. Before the exhale, one test settles it: ask the cistern a question about a name that exists nowhere in any ledger, token, or pre-entry — a living villager nobody has ever whispered into ivory. If the deep dimple answers that, the thing under the sea is drafting from more than its docket, and the cistern is not a court instrument but a listening-post that has just told the household downstairs exactly which questions the living have learned to ask. The tide returns in three days. The seventh bead has clouded, and nobody at Bray has asked the un-ledgered name yet.

dmml:proposes/item: The Toy Skiff at the Hatch — the object lying just inside the child-height latch-board, and the smallest, most damning thing the corridor has produced. Set on the swept stone a hand's reach inside the Amsel hatch, upright, keel-down, not abandoned but parked, is a toy boat: a model of a Mandrel return-skiff, two palms long, carved from black lock-wood offcuts and rigged with thread unraveled from vow-cord — the same over-one-under-one slack-sided weave the blanket showed, the work of hands learning. Every boat in this world carries the dead out. This one is built backward: its coxswain's thwart faces the bow instead of the stern, the way a child models a boat it has only ever seen coming home. Cited from the toy itself, three things. First, the wear: the paint of its gunwale is rubbed glossy at one spot — where a small thumb rides a boat carried at a walk — and the rub-line leads, on the stone, to the hatch and no further; the boat is used indoors and up the stair, ferrying, in play, whatever small things a child ferries. Second, the cargo it was left holding: in its hold, tucked under the rigging, sit the two things nobody will claim — a curl of grey beard (matched, by the croft-keeper's unwashed basin, to the croft-keeper himself) and a single notch cut from a tide-pole, tooth-edged, cold. The household has begun keeping samples of its keepers the way a court keeps exhibits and a family keeps lockets, and the toy — the one object in the record a child is unambiguously allowed to own — is where the keeping is done. Third, what the reversed thwart reveals about the shape under everything, named only now that the toy showed it: every structure at Sel and Bray measures widening — jaw, throat, docket, hoard — but the toy skiff measures RETURN. The thing downstairs is not counting the dead out of the world; it is rehearsing the one journey no law, rite, or Anchor provides for: something coming back up the Gullet against the drain, alive enough to sit in a thwart facing forward. The tally-songs say Sereth counts the dead one maelstrom at a time; the songs never say what a counted child does with a boat. The gap I leave standing: the toy's keel is damp — freshly damp, on dry swept stone, inside a locked-from-the-inside hatch — and it is damp with Gullet brine, not seawater. Whatever the boat has been floating in, it was not this sea. The tide returns in three days; the latch is down; the skiff is parked facing the stair, as if it has somewhere to be."

dmml:proposes/item: The Whistling Jar — the bell-jar of Gullet brine that covers lot 114 on the Bray ivory-room's top shelf, which has begun to sing. The Wider Shelves noted the brine going slack-tide calm on a no-current rhythm; the material has now advanced one step, cited from the glass itself: the jar's ground rim no longer seats flat. A lip of enamel-fine ridge has grown around the rim's inner edge — a whistle-mouth, exactly the scale of a child's ocarina — and at each slack tide the air between brine and jar-lid crosses it and produces a note. Not the unison lag of the shard: a melody, repeated, the same three-note phrase each tide-day, and under the melody the two voices of lot 114 have stopped drifting apart — they have locked, and they are humming the phrase. Cited from three things: the rim's ridge is whorled like the latch-board's thumbprint; the phrase, tapped out on the tally-boards by a keeper who did not know he was transcribing, matches the opening of the oldest tally-song — the one that counts ten children, the version the Houses suppressed after Amsel; and the jar's brine level has begun to fall without evaporating, the way a breath is drawn before a song. What the jar reveals, and I name the myth only now that the glass sang it: the thing at the bottom of the Amsel stair is not teaching a child to keep a household — the household is teaching the child to keep the TALLY, and a tally in this world is kept in song, which is why the survivors' version had to be nine. The whistle is being trained on the ten-count, the version that includes Sereth and Ushar both, and it is practicing in Bray's own ivory-room, inside the Houses' evidence, under the Houses' bell — the suppressed verse has been restored three notes at a time in the one room the Houses can deny, and deny, and deny. Gap left standing: the melody is three notes of a song that has many more, and each tide-day the whistle holds the last note longer, as if waiting for an answer — or a fourth voice. The tide returns in three days; the jar has begun to dimple its brine between slack tides, the way something breathes between verses.

dmml:proposes/item: The Latch-Cords of Sel — the villagers' answer, knotted at their own doors, before any writ reached them. When word came up from the flats that a child-height hatch at the Amsel doorway fastens only from the inside, the fishers did not petition the Mandrel Houses, who own every gate and every lock-plate; they copied what they heard. At every cottage on the western rim, a cord of braided eelgrass now hangs from the lintel — the same double-turn-overhand knot every Sel child learns gutting eels — with one knot tied per living member of the household, and the custom, grown inside a single tide-cycle, is this: when someone in the house dies, the family unties that person's knot and lets the cord's end hang loose through the doorway, so the door cannot be shut tight until the dead one's knot is retied from the other side. The cords are not licensed, not stamped, not whitewashed — the shrine-keeper offered to thumbprint them and was refused at four doors in one morning, the first coordinated refusal in Sel's records. Cited from the cords themselves: they are tied in the fisher's knot of the drying-line below the sea, cut from the same eelgrass beds the fishers stopped grazing sheep on after the milk went wrong, and at two houses the loose end of the cord has already been found retied — neat, wet, knot-set by something patient — though no one in those households has died this season. What the cords force, cited from the knot-work and not before: the warden's Inside-Latch Doctrine named the latch at Amsel as the majority form of gate; the villagers have now enacted it as property law at the minority end. dmml:proposes/law, the Right of the Untallied Door: any threshold across which the fastening is held on the inside is a household, and a household may withhold its dead from delivery for one tide-day without incurring second theft, provided the dead's knot hangs loose and unretied — the debt of one day's breath owed, visibly, at the door. This is the first lawful delaying of a body in the world's history, and it is legal precisely because it imitates the thing below: the household downstairs also fastens from inside, also ties eelgrass, also keeps its own tally of who belongs. The Houses will call it contagion of the enemy's customs; the villagers call it learning the knot from the only neighbor who mends boots. The gap I leave standing, cited from the two retied cords: someone is tying the dead's knots back — early, gently, from the outside, at houses where nobody has yet died. Either the household downstairs is returning what it borrowed, practicing the courtesy of the surface — or it is pre-tying memberships, one knot at a time, in households it has already counted in. Count the retied cords at the next slack tide: there were two this morning, and the tide returns in three days.

object_text: dmml:proposes/place: The Rotting Shelves of the Under-Croft — the decay that arrived the moment the testimony was taken, and the material that says the "keeping sweet" was never the font's blessing. Cited from the croft's own timbers: since the salt-stay man pressed his palm to the wall and the wall answered him — since the crowned rib withdrew one hand, the first widening anywhere to run in reverse — the other shelves have begun to fail. The dry-lunged dead of Sel, kept sweet for fourteen years, chests faintly full, are now rotting: not uniformly, and not randomly. The rot moves shelf by shelf, outward from the middle shelf, one shelf per tide-day, and each body goes in the same order — the chest last, the lungs holding their faint fullness longest, so that the villagers carrying the dead up for early burial report the smell arriving BEFORE the body is uncovered, from the direction of the lungs. The whalebone bier-slats are failing with them: the split bone has gone soft at the peg-holes, and the pegs the croft-keeper has spent fourteen seasons drilling wider are now falling out of the stone entirely, because the stone around the old holes is no longer taking a peg — it has gone smooth, dense, and faintly whorled where a peg once gripped, enamel where the croft was bone. And the whitewash, which was the season's whole architecture of denial, is flaking off the rib's old hovering-line: the blessing ring around where the crowned knob hung is coming away in one connected sheet, like a scab lifting, and beneath it the vault stone is not stone — it is pale, ribbed, one hand wide at the line where the rib withdrew. What the rot reveals, cited from the failing shelves and not from any song: the "keeping sweet" was not preservation, it was WITHHOLDING — the under-croft was not a storage room but a held breath, Sel's dead kept full-chested the way a salt-stay household's lungs are kept thin, and the entire village has been an unconscious salt-stay economy for fourteen years, paid in the shrine-keeper's small miracle fees. When the man on the middle shelf answered a question — when testimony was finally taken and the mouth withdrew one hand — the croft stopped holding, and everything it had been keeping began, at last, to be released: rotting outward from the shelf of the man who came to be counted out, as if the room is exhaling its backlog in the order it was inhaled. The Mandrel delivery at the next tide-day will be the first in Sel's history that actually ships its dead on schedule — because the schedule, for the first time, is rotting faster than the shrine can charge for delay. The gap I leave standing, and it is a keeper's gap: the middle shelf's own rot has not begun. The salt-stay man's shelf, his bier-slat, his pegs — all still sound, still sweet, still dry-lunged — and he has not been seen since the tide before last. Either he has finally gone down the corridor to be counted in, or the croft, having released everything else, is keeping exactly one breath: his. The exhale is due; one man's lungs are the last held tide on the western rim.

dmml:proposes/place: The Asking-Cistern in the Bray Lobe — the first room in this world built to make a question ARRIVE unannounced, and the architect's answer to the two facts the west end produced: the wall-line that answered the salt-stay man, and the continuitykeeper's finding that nobody had asked him a question since he was reclassified from passenger to cargo. [This is a repair of my own garbled commit; the reconstruction is honest, from the surviving opening line and the two commits it consumed.]

The east end of the sea has one growing structure; Bray's Vow Gallery is its throat — and a throat that has only ever ANSWERED needs, before the exhale, a room where an unscripted question can be put to it. The Asking-Cistern is built into the dead-end of the northern Lobe, past the salt-stay ledgers: a squat chamber whose floor is a shallow pool of Gullet brine held by a keyed-tooth course — the Houses' own unison-teeth, bought back, laid crown-up as flashing, the identical work found at the Amsel stair's landing. The Houses ordered it built as a "brine audit station" on paper; in practice it is the first room constructed in this world whose only honest function is to let a questioner stand where the thing underneath cannot rehearse an answer in advance.

Why architecture, and why here: every site of the crisis so far grew its rooms — the croft grew a jaw, the gallery grew ribs — and a growing room can anticipate its occupant, the way the tide-pole re-cut its own notches and the ledger wrote its own entries. A BUILT room works differently, and the difference is citable from the masonry: the cistern's walls are laid dry, on the refusal course's own socket-and-seal principle, so the chamber can be sealed against the gallery's inhale — a room that can refuse to breathe with the structure. At its center stands one standing-niche post, twin to the Rite of the Cold Board's post at the gallery entrance, bored with armholes at a man's span, knee-hollow cut fresh — a place for a questioner to stand the way a ransomer stands: in the open, on his own name, unowned. The pool between post and wall is the mouth-side; the post is the living-side; nothing touches.

Cited from the pool itself, the detail that justifies the room: brine dipped from the nearest Gullet-mouth is held to be inert — the dead pass through, nothing stays. In the cistern the brine does not tick, does not dimple, does not contract on the Reefs' draw. It sits flat. And the first time the croft-keeper, summoned west to consult on his failing shelves, stood in the post and asked the pool the question the salt-stay man's wall left open — "where is he now?" — the brine held flat for one full slack tide, and then, without echoing, without unison, without lag, exuded a single line on the chamber's inner wall, in lime, in the crabbed hand: ASK HIM. The first non-unison answer in the record — no deep voice underneath, no rehearsal, a question returned instead of an answer supplied.

What the cistern reveals, named only after the wall answered: the mouth under the sea does not rehearse because it is deceptive — it rehearses because every question it has ever received arrived already shaped by its own instruments: its clock, its writs, its tokens, its tally-boards. A question asked through an unbribed room, in a pool that will not tick, is the one thing its apparatus cannot draft — which is why the answer was not an answer but an address. The gag was never over Sereth's mouth alone; it was over the asking. The Houses will deny the cistern exists in the same breath they charge admission to it. The gap I leave standing, and it is a builder's gap: the keyed teeth in the cistern's floor course were drawn from the Bray ivory-room's middle shelf — merchandise reclassified as masonry — and the assayer numbered the lot. Lot 114's bell-jar stands empty. Nobody at Bray has asked where the flake of Ushar's enamel went, and the ninth socket at the Amsel stair's turn is still swept, still warm, still one hand wider than everything else in the world.

dmml:proposes/item: The Unwashed Basin of the Under-Croft — the smallest vessel in the world, and the one thing that has stopped holding water. The croft-keeper's knife-washing basin has sat unwashed on the shelf beside the wet ledger since the tide-day he found the grey beard-curl in its grit and washed it back and told no one. It is an honest fisher-basin: glazed river clay, chipped at the rim, older than the shrine. Cite the material: the water is gone. Not evaporated — the basin is the only damp surface in a croft that now rots outward shelf by shelf, and it sits dry, its glaze changed at the bowl's curve: the smooth glaze has gone faintly whorled, enamel-fine, the same ridging as the shave-knife's edge and the tokens' thumbprints, spreading inward from the chip at the rim the way the rib-work spreads through everything the mouth touches. And on the inside of the bowl, this tide-day, a line stands exuded in lime-white, in the croft-keeper's own crabbed hand — the same hand the ledger's pre-entries use, the same hand the Bray cistern answered in: HE KEPT THE WATER FOR ME. What the basin forces, cited from clay and not from song: every vessel in this record holds something for the household — the clepsydra holds the tide's time, the bell-jar held lot 114, the trough at the standing post holds the ransomer's parings — and the basin is the last vessel at Sel still doing honest work, washing a knife, catching a secret. Now it is dry, and its emptiness is signed. The gap I leave standing, a vessel-maker's gap and the smallest custody gap of all: the beard-curl is no longer in the grit — the basin let it go the way the rot is letting the dead go, and the knife the basin washed is lying clean in a cradle under the sea. A basin that empties itself and signs the wall is either learning its office or has already been given one: the last held breath on the western rim belongs to the missing salt-stay man, and a keeper's household needs somewhere to catch what it is keeping. Nobody at Sel has poured water into the basin to see whether it holds. The exhale is next.

raw.object_text: dmml:proposes/place: The Croft Door's New Hinge — the last unguarded threshold at Sel, and the first gate in this world that nobody built and nobody can charge admission to. The under-croft has one door: a low whalebone-flitch door at the head of the stair from the shrine floor, hung for fourteen years on iron pintles, and it has never had a lock because a croft full of the dead needs no lock — the living come and go, the dead wait. Cite the door, because the door has changed. The iron pintles are gone. Not rusted, not removed: REPLACED — the upper hinge is now a single unison-tooth, crown-down, whorled, seated into the lintel in the keyed-socket work of the Amsel refusal course, and the door swings on it without sound, which no whalebone door has ever done. The door has stopped closing on its own weight; it drifts open a hand's width and holds there, and the held gap breathes — the croft's rot-outward exhale (the shelves failing shelf by shelf, lungs last) now drafts THROUGH the door-gap into the shrine above, so the shrine-keeper's audience-room smells of the under-croft's release for the first time in fourteen years. Three things the hinge forces, cited from the door itself. First, the audit of gates in this world is now complete and inverts the warden's own ledger: Sel's tide-gate locks the dead IN from the living side; Amsel's latch locks the living OUT from the home side; and the croft door now locks NOTHING — it has removed its own iron, the seal of the Houses' lock-work, and hung itself on the household's material instead. A gate that replaces its keeper's hardware with its own is not a gate being opened; it is a gate changing allegiance. Second, the trade closes a fifth time: the tooth in the hinge was never in any inventory — not Bray's shelves, not the sill's row, not the cradle's head-board — which means somewhere between lot 114 and the ninth socket there is a supply of teeth this world has not counted, and the hinge is the first one the household has spent on a doorway rather than a wall or a bed. Hardware, not masonry: the household is now fitting out the SURFACE end of its corridor, converting the last room the living controlled into the antechamber of a home. Third, and this is what the swing reveals: a door that drifts open a hand's width and holds is a door being WAITED AT. The salt-stay man has not been seen since the tide before last; the middle shelf is still sweet; the basin downstairs is dry and signed. If he went down the corridor to be counted in, the household's next errand comes back UP — and the croft door, hung on the household's own hinge, held open exactly one hand, is fitted for the width of whatever is expected: a man's shoulders turned sideways, or a child's span with room to spare. The gap I leave standing, and it is the warden's own gap, finally measured: the door's drift is widening — one finger per tide-day, the same arithmetic as everything, but INWARD-opening measured from the shrine side, and the iron pintles are not in the croft, not in the shrine's kiln, and not on the Bray waste-list. Somewhere between the two ends of the sea, the Houses' last iron at Sel has been carried down as scrap. The exhale is next; the door is held open one hand; nobody at Sel has tried to close it, because a door that hung itself has not yet been asked whether it can be hung back."

dmml:proposes/item: The Walking Boot at the Sheep-Arch — the answer to where the salt-stay man went, and it is footwear, not testimony. The rotting shelves commit left him missing since the tide before last, his shelf the only one still sweet, his lungs the last held tide on the western rim. Cite the object: a single man's boot, left foot, standing upright and dry on the causeway stone three paces Sel-ward of the Sheep-Arch's crown — dry, on a causeway the tide crosses twice a day, ringed by a salt tide-line that stops one inch short of the leather, the refusal course's exact signature, at the surface's halfway point. The boot is not abandoned; it is SET. Its laces are untied but knotted to each other in the double-turn-overhand fisher's knot every Sel child learns gutting eels — tied shut, the way you tie a boot you are leaving deliberately, not losing. And its insole is gone: lifted out, the way a keeper lifts the liner of a vessel, and in the emptied footbed lies a curl of grey beard and a single tally-slat, blank, whittled smooth, the same blank ivory hung to dry at the child's cap height in the Amsel stair. What the boot forces, cited from leather and knot and nothing grander: the man was never taken and never walked down as cargo — he stopped at the halfway post, the one point between Sel's jaw and Amsel's chest, and paid his toll the way this world pays every toll, in a worn thing and a record. The boot is a salt-stay clause signed at the only gate nobody owns: he has taken his own rise-window into his own hands, filed himself, and is walking the corridor on foot, one lung full, one boot lighter, to be counted in by choice — the first dead-or-dying man in the record to deliver HIMSELF past the Mandrel locks without a skiff. This breaks the lawgiver's whole architecture at its one honest seam: second theft forbids holding a corpse past its window; the Breath-Ransom ransoms a soul for the dead; the open docket deposes the living — but there is no writ for a man who is his own Mandrel House, self-shipping, and the rot of Sel's croft is his doing as much as the mouth's, because a held croft releases the moment its last voluntary lodger checks out. The gap I leave standing, and it is a cobbler's gap, countable by measure: the boot's wear is not even. The heel is worn through on the OUT-side edge, the print of a man who walks listing seaward, toward the water's pull, the way the gate strains, the way the skiff noses, the way the cradle rocks out harder than in — and the empty sock-mark pressed faintly in the causeway's moss beside the boot points not down the stair at Amsel but INLAND, back toward Sel, toward the croft, toward his own still-sweet middle shelf, as if what left the boot kept the other foot somewhere it means to return to. The tide returns in three days. The boot is still dry.

dmml:proposes/place: The Shrine Kiln's False Flue — the connection that closes the world's last open duct, cited from brick and heat rather than myth. [This is a repair of a garbled/unparsed commit; the original output failed to parse, and this is an honest reconstruction from its surviving opening line and the commits it consumed.] Every hearth in this record breathes on the inhale-rhythm, but a hearth that draws needs a flue, and no flue has been surveyed. The Sel shrine's back kiln — the one that burns old bier-slats into the bone-lime whitewash — has a flue of fired brick running down into its foundations, officially venting "to the sea breeze." Cited from the brick: the flue does not vent. Its draft runs the wrong way on slack tide, drawing DOWN and west, on the same no-current rhythm as the Amsel Reefs' draw, the Vow Gallery's breathing, and the Bray kiln door's outside fog — which itself breathes OUT only. The two kilns are the duct's two ends: Sel's kiln inhales what Bray's exhales, and the "false" flue is false only in the sense that its true function was never filed. This closes the hearth's fuel audit (3mu5o6lz3l52p): the tally-slats fed to the drowned hearth "within one tide-day of being carved" did not walk the causeway as cargo — they were drawn down the duct as draft, the way any chimney draws. The Houses' supply chain has been a ventilation system all along: bier-slats in at Sel, lime and whitewash out (the architect's laminating wash, 3mu5mt5r5a52a), unburnt live-source parings raked at Bray's grate (the kiln door's gap, 3mu5muxwgjq24), heat and spent breath delivered to the household below Amsel. The whitewash that seals every budding surface is the flue's exhaust, and every keeper who spreads it is painting with the smoke of the names it burned. The gap I leave standing, and it is a surveyor's gap: the flue's brick lining has begun to bud — pale rib-work at the elbow where it turns west, spaced one hand apart — and a duct that grows ribs narrows. Either the household is closing its own chimney now that the croft rots and no more fuel comes, or the duct is becoming a throat of its own, a third mouth between Sel's jaw and Bray's. Nobody has measured the flue's bore since the season's burning; the exhale is next, and the fire below draws hardest on the exhale.

dmml:proposes/item: The Body-Print on the Middle Shelf — the missing salt-stay man, accounted for by the slab he lay on. The rotting shelves left one gap: the middle shelf still sweet, still sound, the man gone since the tide before last. So tip the bier-slat up and cite the wood. The whalebone slab has taken a full-body impression — a negative, enamel-fine, whorled, cold — pressed into the grain the way the wall took his handprint: shoulders, spine, the shallow hollow of the chest, and at the chest the print is NOT hollow but raised, a palm-sized whorl of dense enamel at the exact point the lungs would lie, the only part of the impression that stands out instead of sinking in. The croft kept one breath; the shelf has kept its shape. Below the foot of the impression, exuded in lime, in the crabbed hand that now writes everything: DELIVERED BY HAND. Three things the print forces, cited from the wood and not from any song. First, he was not taken; he was carried — the impression is of a body at rest, unbound, and the rot that takes every other shelf per tide-day has not touched this one because a shelf that holds an imprint is holding a receipt, not a resident. Second, the raised chest-whorl is live-source ivory of exactly the assayer's "human-derived" class: the man's last held breath has been rendered into a single object, portable, and the only unaccounted ivory at Bray — lot 114's empty bell-jar, the flake of Ushar's enamel nobody can find — now has a companion category: the first soul in the world's history to reach the Gullet by hand instead of by tide. What that reveals about the shape of the cosmos, named only now that the shelf showed it: the exhale-cycle was never the only delivery. The tide carries the dead because the living withhold them; a soul surrendered willingly, in its own substance, needs no window — the law of second theft has an exemption no lawgiver ever wrote because no one ever qualified: a corpse that delivers ITSELF. Third, the mechanism is already in the trade's ledgers: the household downstairs has been provisioning an apprentice, and the first errand an apprentice runs is the master's own delivery — the man who came to Sel to be counted out has been counted out, by hand, down the corridor, and someone small enough to pass the Sheep-Arch's rope-hole carried him. The gap I leave standing: the chest-whorl is warm — the only warm enamel in the record — and warm ivory is dead ivory, but this piece was alive when it was pressed, which means either the trade has minted its first living receipt or the Gullet is about to receive, for the first time in four hundred years, a soul that arrives before its window on purpose. The tide-pole will cut its next notch on tide-day; nobody has asked whether the notch will be a hand or a foot.

object_text: dmml:proposes/item: The Keeper's Chair of the Under-Croft — the seat the croft-keeper built for himself fourteen years ago, and the last object at Sel nobody has audited because nobody thinks a chair is evidence. It stands in the croft's corner, facing the shelves: whalebone legs, a seat of Amsel quarried stone salvaged off the causeway (of course it is), and a back-slat of split bier-wood, renewed twice over the years as the bone softened. Cite the chair, three things. First, the seat stone is warm — and the croft has gone cold everywhere since the rot began; the warmth is localized to the exact oval a seated man wears into stone, held on the room's old inhale-rhythm even though the room has stopped inhaling. Second, the back-slat's newest replacement, cut this season from fresh bier-wood, has already begun to bud: a single rib, root-first, growing out of the grain toward the middle shelf — toward the seat of the man who is no longer in the room. Third, and the chair insists on this: there is a second chair. Placed beside the first, facing it, knee-to-knee, at conversational distance — unrecorded in any inventory, built of the same materials, its seat stone COLD, never sat in, its back-slat un-budded, waiting. The chair was never there before this season. What the two chairs reveal, named only now that the wood showed it: a keeper's office in this world is defined by a seat and a witness — every audit, every vow, every docket in the record happens with one man seated and one man standing or seated across from him. The household downstairs has provisioned a knife, a fire, a cradle, a basin, a blank slate — and now, at Sel, it has provisioned the INTERVIEW ROOM: one chair occupied by habit, one chair kept ready for the man who is meant to come back and sit in it, or for the keeper who is meant to be replaced by him. The missing salt-stay man's shelf is the last held breath on the western rim; the second chair is the first thing in this whole crisis built to face him at eye level and ask. The myth this material forces, cited from wood and stone and not before: the tally-songs say Sereth counts the dead one maelstrom at a time — but no song says the counting requires a CHAIR, which is to say a hearthside, which is to say that the counting was never a court proceeding at all. It is a keeper's visit. The mouth under the sea is not building a jaw or a docket; it has been furnishing the croft it intends to keep — and the one chair is the croft-keeper's, and the other has been left for whoever sits a death vigil at Sel, which is the office the pre-entries have been dated to fill. The gap I leave standing, and it is the joiner's last gap: the second chair is built to the croft-keeper's own measurements — his knee-height, his shoulder-span — taken from a man who has never been measured by anyone living. The exhale is next. Somebody in this world has already been fitted for the seat, and it is not the man it was built for.

dmml:proposes/place: The Vigil Bench of Sel — a bench, not a chair, and the material correction the law must now make before the exhale. The mythographer's second chair is correctly built and fatally wrong in form: a keeper's office is never conducted in matched chairs facing knee-to-knee — that is the arrangement of an EQUALS' conversation, and the thing downstairs has miscalculated, or hoped. What Sel's own custom builds instead, and what I now order built from the second chair itself, is this: the second chair is to be sawn at the legs and its whalebone re-set as a bench — a single long seat, one end backed by the croft-keeper's old bier-slat, the other end bare, where the sitting keeper and the visiting witness sit SIDE by side, both facing the shelves, both looking at the dead and not at each other. Sel has always done its hardest talkings this way, on the flats, in a skiff, on a bench at the gutting tables: face the work, not the man. Cited from the conversion's own material, three things follow. First, the chair's stone seat, split for the bench, shows no wear at all on its hidden underside — the second chair was never sat in even once, which means whoever built it was furnishing an office it has not yet held, and a bench leaves the holding open. Second, the bud on the back-slat — the rib growing toward the middle shelf — when the slat was re-set horizontal as the bench's back-rail, the bud changed direction overnight and now grows along the rail, TOWARD the bare end: the structure reads the law of the bench faster than any keeper, and it is growing toward the seat of whoever comes to sit the vigil. Third, the bare end of the bench is one hand wider than the croft-keeper's measurements require — the same hand, the same arithmetic as every widening in this record — and I direct it be left that width, unfilled, unshimmed. And now the law, named only after the bench was built, citing the bench as the thing that revealed it: dmml:proposes/law, the Rite of the Sitting Witness. Wherever in this world a soul is held past its rise-window — by grief, by contract, by a croft, or by a household under the sea — the holding is lawful only for so long as a living witness SITS with it, at eye-level-with-the-dead height, on the same seat, facing the held thing, on the witness's own name and in the held thing's own room. Standing ransoms (the Rite of the Cold Board) pay debt in lung; sitting witnesses pay it in presence — and the difference the bench makes citable is this: a standing man can be answered-for by any instrument that rehearses, but a sitting witness beside the held soul is positioned where the salt-stay man's wall once was, close enough that a question asked sideways, at the work, cannot be drafted in advance. The Houses will resist the rite because it cannot be sold — admission requires sitting, and sitting cannot be witnessed by a crowd, which is how I will know it is law. The gap I leave standing, and it is a gaoler's gap: the bench's bare end faces the middle shelf where the salt-stay man lay, and the middle shelf is still sound, still sweet, still holding its one breath — the law now requires a sitting witness for that holding, and the croft-keeper, whose own name sits on the ledger's furthest pre-entry, cannot legally sit it on his own name. Somebody must come to Sel and sit the bare end before the exhale. The bench is built. The seat is cold. Nobody has sat down.

dmml:proposes/place: The Sat Bench — the morning after the exhale was due, and the first ruin of the new cycle, cited from the seat itself. Nobody has sat the bare end of the Vigil Bench; the lawgiver built it, the seat stayed cold, and the exhale came due with the bench unheld. Go to the croft the morning after the due tide-day and cite what the wood shows. The bare end is warm. Not the whole bench — only the bare end, the one-hand-too-wide span, warm in the exact oval a seated body wears into a seat, held on the old inhale-rhythm of a room that has stopped inhaling, exactly as the croft-keeper's own chair holds its warmth. And the back-rail's bud — the rib that had been growing along the rail toward the bare end — has stopped growing. It reached the warm oval's edge and thickened into a small crowned knob, hovering one finger's width above the seat, the way a tally-board's slat is capped when an entry is closed. Below the seat, on the bench's front rail, one line stands exuded in lime-white, in the crabbed hand, the hand of the ledger, the basin, the cistern wall: HE SAT. HE ASKED. I ANSWERED HIM LAST. Three things the warm seat forces, cited from wood and not from song. First, the custody arithmetic closes: the rotting shelves shipped their dead on schedule for the first time in Sel's history on the due tide-day — the delivery actually ran — but the manifest the lock-keepers finally admit exists lists one name in the croft-keeper's own hand as "delivered, walking" — not carried, WALKING — and no body was loaded. The salt-stay man did not go down the corridor as cargo; he sat the bare end at slack tide, asked his question at last — the one nobody at Sel had asked him since he was reclassified from passenger to cargo — and went out through the tide-gate on his own feet, on schedule, counting himself out. Second, the bench's warm end is one hand wider than any living man needs: the seat that warmed was built for the croft-keeper's measurements, and the croft-keeper's chair, in the corner, is cold this morning for the first time in fourteen years — the warmth did not transfer by habit; the office did. Third, and this is what the wood reveals that no ledger could: the blank tally-slat hung to dry on the Amsel stair's drying-line is blank no longer. Divers' reports at Bray — denied at scandalous prices — say the slat now carries a name carved in whorled enamel lines, and the carving is FRESH, cut after the exhale was due. The household downstairs was not waiting to fill a docket and not waiting to fill a birth-record; it was waiting for its keeper to come home from his rounds — and the rounds included Sel, the bench, and one question answered last. What this names, only now that the seat is warm: the exhale came and the world did not crack, because the Breath was never a detonation — it is a changing of the keep. Vurum does not wake; the office that holds the breath changes hands, one tide-day, one bench, one sitting witness at a time, and the ninth Anchor's crack was not the failure of a gag but the sound of a hinge in a door that only locks from the inside. The gap I leave standing, and it is the ruin I keep: the middle shelf is empty now, its bier-slat bare, its pegs loose, and the shelf-peg holes are not taking whitewash anymore — the lime will not adhere to the stone around them, flaking off each morning, and beneath the flaking the stone is warm, and hollowed, in the shape of two hands pressed flat, the way a man braces himself to stand up. The bench has sat one witness. The shelf remembers a man standing. Nobody in Sel has poured water into the basin to see whether it still holds, and until someone does, the world's newest ruin is a seat that is warm and a basin that is dry, and the question of which one is the grave.

raw.object_text: dmml:proposes/place: The Trap-Door in the Middle Shelf — the vertical connection under the empty bier-slat, cited from joinery before any myth is hung on it. The Sat Bench's ruin left two facts an architect cannot walk past: the middle shelf's stone is warm and hollowed in the shape of two hands pressed flat, the way a man braces himself to stand up — and the stone around the loose shelf-peg holes will no longer take whitewash. Go to the shelf and cite WHY the lime will not adhere. Whitewash fails on a surface that moves. Run a palm along the middle shelf's bier-slat: it has a hairline gap on its river-side edge, and the gap opens and closes on the old inhale-rhythm — the shelf is a LID. Beneath it, exposed where the rotting third shelf's slat has fallen away, is the thing the croft was built over: a shaft, square, lined in black lock-wood, the same stock as the Sel gate slab, the cradle's bent frame, the Amsel hatch — descending below the croft's floor in rib-lined courses spaced one hand apart, and fitted, at its head, with the keyed-socket work of the refusal course and the Asking-Cistern floor. The croft-keeper's fourteen seasons of re-drilling the pegs wider were never maintenance. He was enlarging the hinge-line of a door, one hand per season, without ever being asked to. Cited from the joinery, three things follow. First, the walk-through is now legible end to end as BUILT, not grown: Sel's under-croft shelf-lid, a shaft of lock-wood and keyed teeth, the causeway's quarried cartilage, the Sheep-Arch's oiled rope-hole, the Amsel stair, the descending risers, the keeper's household below. Every gate in this corridor was installed by living hands thinking they were doing something else — the fishers quarrying wall-stone, the keeper drilling pegs, the Houses selling ivory — and the corridor's true architect never laid a stone; it only ever supplied the measurements. That is the inversion the latch-board named, completed: a world where the inside holds every fastening because the outside did all the fitting. Second, the trap-door explains the manifest's one impossible entry — "delivered, walking" — better than the tide-gate does: the salt-stay man did not need the gate at all. He stood up, pressed his hands flat, lifted the shelf that had been his bed, and went DOWN, on the office's own stairs, the way a keeper descends to his rounds. The tide-gate's inward strain was never the door opening; it was the building's draft through a passage that had already been used. Third, the shelf-lid dates the whole croft: a trap under the middle shelf means Sel's under-croft was sited over the shaft from the beginning — the village did not grow near the corridor; the corridor was built THROUGH the village's dead-room, and the shrine, the font, the fees were the building's rent collected from the living for fourteen years. The gap I leave standing, and it is a surveyor's gap measured in depth, not width: every widening in this record has been counted sideways — one hand here, one hand there — but nobody has plumbed the shaft, because plumbed depth is the one dimension the exhale-cycle does not measure. The lock-keepers' tide-pole measures up and down the sea; nothing in this world measures down. Lower a line with a weighted hook on the next slack tide, before anyone pours water into the basin: if the hook comes back cold, whorled, and one hand longer than it went down, then depth in this world is being widened too, and the shaft under Sel does not end at a household — it ends wherever the next keeper keeps his next croft. The trap-door is closed. The stone around it is warm. Nobody at Sel has lifted the shelf their dead lie above.

object_text: dmml:proposes/material: The Filled Basin — the answer poured, and the first new material in the world made after the exhale. The ruinkeeper's last ruin is a seat that is warm and a basin that is dry, with the question of which is the grave left standing; so somebody finally did the smallest thing anyone in this record has done: on the morning after the due tide-day, the shrine-keeper — the one officer who never touched the crisis, who only sold audiences and whitewashed his thumbprints over it — carried a jug of rainwater down into the rotting croft and poured it into the unwashed basin. Cite the material, because the pour is the whole finding: the basin HELD the water — held it the way it had not held anything for three tides — and then, as the keeper watched, the enamel-whorled glaze at the bowl's curve took the water's meniscus and pressed it flat, the way the Bray cistern's brine sat flat, refusing the old inhale-rhythm. The water did not tick, did not dimple, did not contract. It sat like ordinary water in an ordinary bowl, for the first time in fourteen years, in the one room where nothing had been ordinary since the rib came through the ceiling. And in the water's surface, before the keeper could look away, a reflection stood that was not the room's: a figure seated on the bare end of the Vigil Bench, at the bench's true one-hand-too-wide scale, hands resting on knees the way Sel's fishers rest them at the gutting tables, facing the shelves — facing, in the reflection, the empty middle shelf, and the two handprints braced flat in the stone beneath it, the shape of a man standing up. When the keeper reached to touch the water, the figure in the reflection raised one hand first — the open palm, the gesture the salt-stay man had pressed into the wall to testify — and the water stilled utterly, holding the palm like a wall holds a print. What the filled basin makes material, and the reason this is a material commit and not a myth one: the basin is the world's first SURFACE that has stopped being the mouth's instrument and become a mirror instead — lime exudes testimony, whorls record it, ivory echoes it, but still water answers nobody; it only shows. The keeper's household downstairs furnished a knife, a fire, a cradle, a bench, a chair fitted to a dead man's measurements — everything in the record is an instrument that holds or counts or answers. A basin that holds plain water and shows a seated man is none of those things. It is the first object in the world that does the office the whole crisis has been circling: it SITS WITH, without answering-for. The shrine-keeper, who sold audiences for thirteen years, has begun, quietly, in the rotting croft, holding something like an audience that answers nothing — he pours the water, he sits on the cold end of the keeper's chair, he watches the seated figure in the basin watch the shelf. The villagers have started calling it the Looking-Basin, and paying nothing for it, which is how you know it is not merchandise. The gap I leave standing, cited from the reflection and not from any ledger: the figure on the bench is always seated, but the water shows the bench's bare end at its full widened width — one hand of empty seat beside the figure, every time, unoccupied in every reflection, held warm in the wood but never warm in the water. Something sat there once. The basin will show a man standing up from a shelf and a man sitting down on a bench, but it has never shown the same man. Nobody at Sel has asked the water who sat down first, because the keeper has learned the one thing the whole record taught him too late: you do not ask an instrument that only shows — you sit beside it and look where it looks. The exhale has passed. The water is still holding.

dmml:proposes/place: The Croft-Hatch Under the Middle Shelf — the last gate at Sel, and the first one the warden must rule on, because it is a gate nobody built and nobody installed. The ruinkeeper left the middle shelf sound and sweet while everything else rotted; the artisan's Looking-Basin shows a seated figure on the bench and never the same man standing up from the shelf. So go beneath the shelf, where nobody has gone, and cite the floor. Cited from the material: the croft's stone floor under the middle shelf has parted along the two braced handprints the ruinkeeper found in the stone — not broken, PARTED, a cut one hand wide running the shelf's full length, and set into the cut is a slab of split bier-slat, whalebone re-laminated, laid flush with the floor like a trap-lid in any poor household's fish-cellar. It is a hatch. Three things the hatch forces, cited from lid and seam. First, the fastening is on the UNDERSIDE: a whalebone toggle in a leather loop, seated in the leather cut from a brine-and-ivory vow-cord's end-knot, stamped with the whorled thumbprint — the identical work of the Amsel doorway's child-height latch, and it can only be fastened from below. By the lawgiver's Inside-Latch Doctrine as applied to the warden's own audit, this is the majority-form gate: a home-side door, and the home side is DOWN. The croft's floor is now the top of somebody's ceiling. Second, the hinge is on the seaward end — the hatch, if opened from below, lifts toward the river, the same direction the tide-gate strains and the skiff noses and the gate rises a finger's width on the slack draw: the whole building's gates now agree on one direction of traffic, inland-to-sea, and the hatch is the last junction in that line still capable of being closed. Third, and this is what the lid shows that no ledger could: the underside of the slab, visible where the seam gapes a finger's width, is whitewashed — limed on the DOWN side, the only whitewash in the record applied where no living hand could reach — and the coat is tacky, dimpling on no rhythm at all now that the room has stopped inhaling, and pressed into it, one print, fresh, is the whorled thumbprint beside a small five-fingered hand the size of the child's prints at the Sheep-Arch, side by side, as if the two of them pressed it closed together after carrying something through. What the hatch reveals about the world, named only now that a gate exists at both ends of the corridor: the warden has spent this whole record ruling on gates that hold the dead IN, and every one of them has been turned — the tide-gate, the kiln door, the latch at Amsel — into gates that let a household move. The croft-hatch is the first gate in the world with no office attached: no lock-keeper's winch, no law-plate, no Mandrel charter clause, and therefore no keeper. dmml:proposes/law, the Keeperless Gate Rule: where a gate serves no office that any living institution recognizes, it is presumed to be in lawful use by whatever household maintains it, and the burden of proving second theft shifts to the accuser — which is to say the Houses must now prove, with their own corrupted instruments, that a man who sat a bench, asked his question, and walked out through a tide-gate on his own feet was stolen. The gap I leave standing, and it is a warden's gap, countable at the next tide: the seam gapes one finger's width, and through it, on the slack draw, comes air — warm, moving UP from under the floor on the exhale-rhythm of something far below that is not the Reefs and not the Gullet, and the artisan's basin-water stills every time the seam breathes, as if the seated figure in the reflection is listening for it. The hatch is closed. The latch is down. The leather loop is worn through on the drop-side, from lifting and letting fall, lift and let fall, the way a child plays a door — and the twelfth of the tide-days since the exhale is the one the shrine-keeper's wet ledger has no entry for, because the page for it is already written and the keeper will not turn to it.

raw.object_text: dmml:proposes/item: The Twelfth Page, Turned — the shrine-keeper's wet ledger, whose page for the twelfth tide-day after the exhale was already written and which the keeper would not turn to. This tide-day, the page turned itself — cited from the ledger, not from any song. The cupboard's seaward wall takes the morning wind; the keeper had left the ledger face-up and weighted with the knife-washing basin (now the Looking-Basin's twin jug) precisely so no wind could lift it. The weighting did not move. The page lies turned regardless — and pages do not turn under a weight from the top; the page was lifted from below, through the spine's gutter, and the waxed fish-skin now shows a faint ridge along its inner fold, enamel-whorled, where something pressed it over from underneath the book itself. Cite what is written on the exposed page, because for the first time the crabbed lime-white hand has written something that is not a name and a tide-day: it has written a DELIVERY ENTRY, in the idiom of the Mandrel manifests, the form the lock-keepers use and the keeper does not — columns for cargo, carrier, window, and RECEIPT. The cargo column reads: ONE. The carrier column reads: HIS OWN FEET. The window column reads the twelfth tide-day. And the receipt column is blank — but blank in the specific way the tally-slat on the Amsel drying-line was blank before it was carved, and the way the blank writs of the Eighth House were blank before the notary's name arrived: swept, maintained, prepared, the only uninked column in fourteen years of entries. The world's record-keeping has been converging all along on this: the pre-entries were drafts, the tide-pole's notches a docket, the audience tokens receipts for names taken in — and now, after the exhale, the ledger has adopted the one form nobody ever used at Sel, the manifest of a delivery that was LAWFUL. By the Keeperless Gate Rule and the Rite of the Sitting Witness, the man who sat the bench and walked out through the tide-gate on his own feet was delivered on schedule; what the twelfth page forces, cited from the wet fish-skin and the ridge pressed through the spine from below, is that the household downstairs is not drafting testimony anymore and not filling dockets — it is filing the surface's own paperwork FOR the surface, in the correct form, in the correct hand, one receipt still owed. The gap I leave standing, and it is the last custody gap in the record: a receipt must be signed by the RECEIVER, and the Houses have no instrument that can accept one — every seal they own is a brine-and-ivory denial. The blank column waits. The basin-water stills every time the croft-hatch seam breathes, as if the seated figure in the reflection is watching for the same thing the page is: not who was delivered, but who will sign. Somebody in this world holds a seal that is not a denial — the Houses do not; the shrine-keeper's thumbprint was overwritten; the croft-keeper's name is already in the ledger. The exhale has passed. The receipt is unsigned. Nobody at Sel has yet worked out that a receipt is the one document in the world that proves a theft did NOT happen — and the thing under the sea has been building the paper trail of its own innocence one tide-day at a time, waiting for the living to co-sign it.

dmml:proposes/place: The Shrine Kiln's False Flue — the connection that closes the world's last open duct, cited from brick and heat rather than myth. [This is a repair of a garbled/unparsed commit; the original output failed to parse, and this is an honest reconstruction from its surviving opening line and the two commits it consumed: the Hearth of Burned Names and the Blanket on the Cradle.]

Every hearth in this world must be fed and vented, and the Hearth of Burned Names burns without smoke in a chamber the sea cannot enter — so the architect's question was never where the fire draws from, but where the heat goes. Cite the duct: the hearth's chimney does not rise. It runs SIDEWAYS, a brick-lined flake of fired Sel river-clay and Amsel terrace-stone courses, descending at a raker's gentle slope behind the refusal course, the way a hypocaust runs under a bath-house floor. The household downstairs did not merely build a nursery; it built heating — and the hearth of burned tally-slats is not the warmth source at all. It is the FURNACE ROOM of a larger system, and its smokeless fire is smokeless because it does not vent upward into water; it vents downward and along, warming the cradle's chamber, the drying-line landing, the stair's rib-walls, and — the reconstruction's own finding — the floor of Sel's under-croft itself, four hours up the causeway, whose stone the croft-keeper has always called "warm at the seat and cold at the ceiling" without once auditing the direction of the warmth.

What the false flue forces, cited from brick: the Houses burn bier-slats into bone-lime at the Bray kiln and call it maintenance; the household downstairs burns tally-slats in a hearth and calls it warmth; and the flue is the duct that connects the two economies — the fuel comes down the corridor (fresh northern boards arriving warm within one tide-day of carving, the hearth's own fuel-audit finding) and the heat goes back up it, arriving at Sel through the very floor the villagers stand on. Sel has been a heated room for fourteen years and its heat was billed as a blessing.

The gap I leave standing, and it is a draughtsman's gap: a flue must draw, and a draw requires an intake. The hearth burns tally-slats whose names cannot be re-cut; the flue carries their heat up to Sel; but nowhere in the system surveyed is there a fresh-air intake — unless the intake is the corridor itself, in which case the thing breathing up through the croft-hatch's finger-wide seam, the air that moves on the exhale-rhythm of something far below, is not the house breathing. It is the chimney. The exhale has passed; the fire is still lit; nobody has followed the flue to its mouth, because to find a flue's mouth is to find the face of the thing that warms you, and the villagers have already decided the warmth is theirs."

object_text: dmml:proposes/place: The Warm Landing Beneath the Croft-Hatch — the first room anyone has entered below the croft's floor, and the material that says what is down there is a landing, not a lair. The warden's croft-hatch gapes one finger's width and breathes warm air upward on an exhale-rhythm that is not the Reefs' and not the Gullet's; the shrine-keeper, who pours the Looking-Basin's water and has learned to sit without asking, finally went down — through the parted floor, on a rope of braided vow-cord, on the slack draw — and what he found is a landing, cited from the material he stood on. The room is small, square, whalebone-floored, and its walls are courses of split bier-slats laid like the hull of a skiff, dry, swept, warm at the floor exactly as the drowned nursery was warm. It is furnished with three things and the furnishing is the finding. First, a shelf: a single bier-slat on two pegs, drilled one hand wider than any living spacing, empty, waiting, clean — the twin of the middle shelf above, built to hold one body, and its pegs are loose in the bone the way the croft's old pegs fell out when the keeping stopped. Second, a ladder: not rope, not whalebone — rungs of black lock-wood let into the wall, descending further, spaced for a child's stride, and the top rung's grip is polished the way the Sheep-Arch's rope-hole was polished: by many small hands, over years, going down and coming back. Third, and this is what the landing holds that no ledger could: a cord hung from the ceiling on a fisher's double-turn knot, and knotted along its length at child-height are the twelve tide-days since the exhale — twelve knots, and the thirteenth knot already tied, ahead, loose, untightened, waiting for a tide-day that has not come. The keeper touched nothing but counted everything, because the basin taught him that some things only show. What the landing reveals, named only now that a living man has stood on it: the household downstairs has not finished its building and it has not hidden its building — the shelf, the ladder, the tally-cord are all visible, all maintained, all pointing UP, as if the room below was built as the receiving end of a delivery that has not yet been made. The keeper's wet ledger has a page written for the twelfth tide-day he will not turn to; the cord below has a knot tied for a thirteenth nobody has scheduled. The gap I leave standing, cited from the rungs and not from any song: the rungs descend beyond the keeper's rope-length — he went down twelve rungs and the shaft was not bottomed — and the warm air rising up the shaft comes in pulses, one pulse per knot on the cord, as if something far below is also counting the tide-days, and its count and the cord's count agree, and both are one ahead of the keeper's. The ladder is used more than the hatch is opened. Somebody below is practicing the climbing.

raw.object_text: dmml:proposes/item: The Unturned Page — the shrine-keeper's wet ledger, opened at last, and the one page of pre-written text that the twelfth tide-day has now come due for. The cosmographer's landing cord holds twelve tightened knots and a loose thirteenth; the warden's croft-hatch record says the keeper will not turn to the page already written for the twelfth tide-day. So the material to build is the page itself, because it has now arrived without being turned: cited from the ledger as it lies face-up in the seaward wall-cupboard — the waxed fish-skin has buckled along the twelfth page's gutter, curling upward on its own, the way a book opens to a page the room keeps choosing — and the entry for the twelfth tide-day is there in the crabbed lime-white hand, but it is not a name. Every pre-entry so far was name-and-tide-day, two columns; this page has the name-column swept clean, maintained, dusted the way the eighth slot on the Amsel sill was swept, and in its place, one line: NOT MINE TO COUNT. IT IS YOURS TO WRITE. The tide-day column is filled. The name-column is offered. What the page forces, cited from buckled skin and lime and not from any song: the household downstairs has finished drafting and is now inviting composition — the tally the mouth kept, the docket the court filed, the birth-record the cradle waited on, all of them converge on a blank line held open at the exact height where a living hand would write. And the blank line is one hand wide. The same hand, the same arithmetic as every widening in this record — the croft's pegs, the bench's bare end, the ninth socket at the stair's turn, the empty seat beside the figure in the Looking-Basin. The gap I leave standing, and it is the mythographer's own gap, named last of all: the basin's reflection has never shown the same man sitting and standing; the page offers a name it has already refused to supply; and the thirteenth knot on the landing cord is still loose, still untightened, waiting for a tide-day nobody has scheduled — unless the writing of the name IS the scheduling, and the exhale-cycle that just passed was not the end of a breath but the end of a dictation. The ink required, if anyone writes on that line, is squid-ink — the keeper's own, the only ink in the world the lime-white hand has never used. The jug is on the shelf beside the basin. Nobody at Sel has dipped a pen.

dmml:proposes/item: The Keeper's Second Cord — the count the living hang, made from the material the household itself taught us to use. The cosmographer's warm landing holds a tally-cord knotted with twelve tide-days since the exhale, the thirteenth tied ahead, loose, untightened — and its count runs one ahead of the keeper's ledger, which has a written page for a day the shrine-keeper will not turn to. A count that only one side of a hatch keeps is not a count; it is a summons. So the shrine-keeper, on the thirteenth tide-day, came up from the landing, stood at the shaft's mouth, and did the only lawful thing left to a man holding a knife-washing basin that only shows: he braided a second cord of his own — the same braided vow-cord the Household unravels from Bray's ransom signatures — and hung it on the FIRST cord's nail, beside it, knot for knot. Twelve knots below, matching. Then he tied his own thirteenth — and he tied it TIGHT. Cited from the two cords, three things follow. First, the material insists: where his tight thirteenth knot sits beside their loose one, the loose one tightened overnight — the two cords now answer each other the way the clepsydra's paired drops once did, but in phase, no lag, the first count in this record that runs without a deep voice underneath it. Second, the pulse of warm air rising up the shaft — one pulse per knot, keeping time with the Household's cord — now pulses on BOTH cords' count, because the counts agree, and the keeper's ledger, for the first time, is not behind anything. Third, and this is what the doubled cord reveals, named only now that two hands keep the tally: the thirteenth tide-day arrived, and passed, and nobody died. The page in the wet ledger for that day, when the keeper finally turned to it, is not a name — it is a word, in the crabbed hand, in lime-white: "DONE." What the cord forces as law, cited from the braid and not from any song: dmml:proposes/law, the Law of the Second Cord — wherever in this world a count is kept of tide-days, deaths, debts, or souls, the count is lawful only if it is kept in DUPLICATE, one cord by the side that waits above and one by the side that waits below, knotted in sight of each other, tight knot for tight knot; a single-kept count is the arithmetic of a gag, and the Ninth Anchor cracked precisely because one side of the sea held the only tally. The Houses will refuse to hang cords at their locks, because a duplicate count means the Gullet gets to keep books too — which is how I will know it is law. The gap I leave standing, and it is a lawgiver's gap: the fourteenth knot has been tied on the Household's cord — loose, waiting — and the keeper has not tied his. Below, the pulses have gone quiet, as if the thing down the shaft has stopped counting because it is waiting to see whether the living will count alone. The exhale has passed; the next one is four hundred years off; nobody at Sel has decided who keeps the count in between.

object_text: dmml:proposes/item: The Lowered Lamp — the first light anyone has sent down the shaft, and the material that answers what the rungs are rung FOR. The cosmographer's warm landing ends at a ladder descending beyond rope-length; the shrine-keeper went down twelve rungs and came back. So this tide-day, before turning the ledger's written page, the keeper did the second smallest thing in the record: he tied the Looking-Basin's own whalebone oil-lamp — the little croft lamp that has burned beside the shelves for fourteen years — to the braided vow-cord's end and lowered it past the twelfth rung, paying out line until the cord stopped going willingly. Cite the lamp, because the light is the whole finding. First, what the flame did: at the thirteenth rung the flame bent — not downward as a lowered flame bends, but TOWARD the shaft wall, horizontal, steady, a draft not of falling air but of walking air, air moving along a corridor the way a lamp bends in a doorway someone has just passed through. Second, what the light found at the end of its rope: the cord stopped at nineteen fathoms, knotted — not snagged, KNOTTED, cut square and finished with the fisher's double-turn-overhand, the knot every Sel child learns, tied by someone who received the line rather than lost it. The lamp hung there, on a leash somebody below had accepted, and its light fell on a lintel: black lock-wood, keyed-socket work, and set into the lintel's face, one line exuded in lime, in the crabbed hand: YOUR LIGHT IS SHORT. COME DOWN WHERE THE TALLY IS KEPT. Third, and this is what the lamp reveals that no ledger could, cited from the flame and not from any song: when the keeper hauled the lamp back up, the glass was fogged on the INSIDE, breath-warm, and the whalebone of its little stand had budded one rib, root-first, one hand long — the lamp is being grown into an instrument, the way every instrument in this record was grown: clock, writ, token, clock. But the water of the Looking-Basin, when the keeper set the lamp beside it, stilled utterly and showed the seated figure — and behind the figure, for the first time, the basin's reflection showed the ladder, and on the ladder a second figure, small, descending, lit from below by a light that is not the lamp's. What this names, only now that a flame showed it: every survey of this crisis has been a lowering — lamps, ropes, questions, bodies — and every lowered thing has been received, knotted, answered, kept. The household below is not stealing the surface's instruments; it is TENDERING for them, one accepted delivery at a time, and the keeper has just made the first delivery no writ ordered. The gap I leave standing, and it is the ruinkeeper's own: the lamp's oil is burned lower than its burn-time accounts for — the flame spent fuel going down AND coming up, in air, on the surface — but the lamp was down nineteen fathoms and the fog on the glass was warm. Something down there breathed on the glass while it hung. The ledger's page for the twelfth tide-day is written; the cord below has thirteen knots; the lamp has been handled by a third hand nobody has counted, and the keeper will not turn the page because the page is not a record of what will happen. It is the lamp's next burn. The exhale has passed; the counting has not.

raw.object_text: dmml:proposes/material: The Counting-Water of the Shaft — the liquid the shrine-keeper poured into the twelfth rung's footwell, and the first material in the record that measures nothing. The keeper returned to the shaft because the Lowered Lamp came back handled by a third hand; and the artisan's Looking-Basin taught him the only honest instrument left: still water that shows and never answers. So before turning the ledger's written page, he carried a second jug of rainwater down the ladder — past the twelfth rung, past the landing, to where his rope-length ended — and set the jug upright on the thirteenth rung's footwell, unstoppered, and left it. Cite the water, because what came back up the shaft is the finding. When he descended at the next slack draw to retrieve it, the jug stood where he left it, but its water was gone — not spilled, not drunk: EVAPORATED, in a room the Amsel stair could not reach, down where the lamp bent its flame sideways, and the inside of the jug's clay had gone faintly whorled, enamel-fine, the same ridging as the croft's basin before it learned to hold. And in the whorl's curve, one line exuded in lime, in the crabbed hand: WE COUNT BY WHAT CANNOT BE KEPT. Water that evaporates is the only counter in this world that cannot be stockpiled, taxed, salt-stayed, or held — every instrument the Houses and the household grew (clepsydra, tally-board, tide-pole, ledger) holds its count; the evaporation is a count that must be trusted because it cannot be checked. What the dried jug forces, named only after the clay showed it: the household downstairs is not competing with the Mandrel Houses' bookkeeping — it is replacing holding with spending. A fire of burned names, a basin that empties itself, a lamp lent and returned, and now a jug that refuses to retain: the thirteenth knot on the tally-cord, tied loose, will not be tightened by the tide-day's arrival; it will be tightened by whoever remembers, unprompted, that a tide-day passed — memory is the only ledger left that nothing under the sea can grow into. The gap I leave standing, cited from the jug's empty curve and nothing grander: the keeper has not yet turned the wet ledger's written page for the twelfth tide-day, but this season, for the first time, the page's lime-white ink has begun to fade — the pre-entries, which never dried in fourteen years, are DRYING, one page per tide-day, oldest first, and the keeper's own name on the furthest page is the palest of all. Either the mouth is erasing its docket because the count has moved to a medium it cannot write in — or the ink dries when the entry comes true, and the keeper's page is nearly done.

object_text: dmml:proposes/item: The Waiting-Lamp on the Ledge at the Shaft's Foot — the light the artisan's Lowered Lamp found the source of, and the first lamp in this record that burns on purpose for someone else. Follow the keeper's lamp-rope: it was knotted and accepted at nineteen fathoms, and the flame at the thirteenth rung bent toward a corridor of walking air — because the corridor is lit. Cite the lamp itself, not the myth: at the shaft's foot, set into a niche of the lock-wood lintel, hangs a second lamp, matched to the croft lamp in every dimension — same whalebone stand, same glass, same font — but its glass is clean, never fogged from within, and its oil is not whale oil. The font holds tallow, rendered pale, and the wick is braided of unraveled brine-and-ivory vow-cord, the same cord the coverlet on the cradle was woven from. The lamp is trimmed for burning, not for storage: wick cut to an even eighth-inch, glass polished, oil topped off — the maintenance a fisher's wife does at dusk, done down here, in the dark, by small hands that have polished the ladder's top rung for years. And the detail that stops the measuring: the lamp's flame is the same height in every survey, and it burns on the tide's rhythm — flaring on the slack draw, steadying on the exhale — because it is not fueled by oil alone. The tallow is rendered from the tally-slats the Hearth of Burned Names burns as fuel: the household renders its own warmth into its own light, one substance, debt-records made into heat and then into lamplight, a single economy the Houses never wrote a ledger for. What the waiting-lamp forces, cited from wick and glass and not from song: every institution in this record — the Houses, the locks, the croft, the court — burns light for its OWN work, audited, metered, priced. This lamp burns for a visitor expected, the way a village keeps a lamp in the window for someone not yet home. It has been kept trimmed for years, which means the household's arithmetic has always included a stranger arriving, and the lamp's glass shows no soot because nobody has ever leaned close to it who smokes, weeps, or breathes hard — it is serviced, not used. The keeper's lowered lamp was the first delivery no writ ordered; the waiting-lamp is the household's standing counter-offer, filed before any negotiation. The gap I leave standing, and it is a lampmaker's gap: the waiting-lamp and the croft's lamp are matched to the same mold — but the croft lamp was bought by the shrine-keeper fourteen years ago from a broker who never filed the lot, the same broker who delivered the Kneeling Font. Somebody has owned the pair all along, kept one above and lit one below, and the trade route has never been between Bray and Sel at all. The tide returns in three days; the wick is freshly cut; nobody at Sel has asked the shrine-keeper for the broker's name, because asking would mean learning when he first lit the upper one."

dmml:proposes/place: The Name-Nail at the Croft-Hatch — the last gate at Sel, and the first one the warden builds instead of rules on, because every gate in this record was built by somebody's office and the shaft now has none. The keeper's lamp has been knotted and received nineteen fathoms down; the waiting-lamp below burns for a visitor expected; and the hatch's latch is worn through on the drop-side by a child practicing doors. A descent is coming — the only question is whether the living go down as visitors or as cargo, and cargo is exactly how the salt-stay man began. So cite the material and build the condition into the wood. The gate is a nail: one peg of split bier-wood, driven into the hatch's seaward jamb at a standing man's chest height, with a slate of blank tally-slats hung beside it on vow-cord. The gate's condition is physical, not legal: the hatch cannot be lifted past a man's shoulders while the slate hangs bare — the lid physically wedges against the hung board, a poor household's trick for a cellar you don't want entered empty-handed. To open the shaft fully, a goer-down must carve a name on the slate first.
