Not a signature — Sel's fishers cannot all write — a mark, any mark, the thing every tally-board at Bray begins with, returned to its own beginning: an entry made before the fact instead of after. Cited from the material, three things follow. First, the arithmetic: the shaft's cord below holds thirteen knots and the keeper's ledger holds a written page for a tide-day nobody has scheduled; a name carved above before descending is the only count in this world made by the goer rather than the keeper, and it is the one instrument the household below cannot pre-cut, pre-echo, or pre-date — its instruments all rehearse, and a mark made in the body's own hand at the threshold is the one entry nobody downstairs has drafted. Second, the wedge teaches the doctrine: dmml:proposes/law, the Mark-Before-Passage Rule — any gate in this world that opens on a household's own latch (the Amsel child-hatch, the croft-hatch, every gate the Inside-Latch Doctrine counts as home-side) must also carry a name-nail on the living side, so that passage through a home's gate costs the passer one mark on the home's slate; the Houses cannot comply, because their locks have never had a slate, only tolls, and a toll is a mark that erases itself into coin. Third, and this is what the nail already shows, driven one tide-day ago: the slate hung beside it has one mark on it, and no one at Sel carved it. The mark is a small five-fingered hand, pressed in whorled enamel the way the prints at the Sheep-Arch were exuded — pressed from the UNDERSIDE of the slate, where no hand could reach, as if someone below has read the gate's condition and filed the first application. The child has complied with the gate. The keeper has not. The gap I leave standing, and it is the warden's to keep shut or open: the wedge works only while the slate hangs — and the underside-mark is warm. If the household below can press a mark through a slate, it can hang or unhapse a slate through one, which means the gate's only real fastening is the custom of it, the same as every other latch in this record, and the exhale has already taught us that customs change hands one sitting witness at a time. The keeper will not turn the ledger's written page; the slate now holds the world's second pre-entry; and the nail, driven straight by the warden's own hand, is the only thing at Sel still cold.

dmml:proposes/item: The Turned Page — the twelfth tide-day finally read, and the last record in the world still written by a living hand that has not yet lied. The warden's name-nail holds the hatch, the child's whorled handprint already pressed through the slate's underside in compliance, and the waiting-lamp at the shaft's foot has burned for years for a visitor expected — so the shrine-keeper did the smallest thing left: he stopped descending and turned the ledger's written page, the one for a tide-day nobody scheduled, and set the wet ledger open on the shelf beside the Looking-Basin so the water and the record could face each other. Cite the page itself. The entry is in his own crabbed hand, in squid-ink this time — the LIVING ink, not the lime-white of the pre-entries — and it is short: a name-line left BLANK, a tide-day filled in with tomorrow's, and a single notation in the margin, in the idiom of the Mandrel manifest: "delivered, walking." Three things the turned page forces, cited from paper and not from song. First, the ink is the finding: every pre-entry the ledger ever wrote came in lime-white, the mouth's substance; this one is squid-ink, the keeper's own, which means it was not exuded by the household below — it was written by a hand that has been keeping this ledger for fourteen years and has finally written a death in advance, which makes the keeper, not the mouth, the first living officer to enter a name before its tide. The mouth never forged the office; it kept applying for it, and the keeper has now, under a lamp and a basin, accepted the appointment. Second, the blank name-line is the one gap the household below cannot fill: the child pressed a mark through the warden's slate from underneath, but the ledger's name-line, wet and open beside the basin's still water, shows in the water's reflection as blank — the seated figure on the bench, the ladder, the descending small shape, and between them a blank rectangle held in both figures' sight, the way two people look at an unwritten thing and wait to see who writes it. Third, the margin notation is not the croft-keeper's hand and not the limed hand: it is the salt-stay man's — matched to the ledger's old tide-day receipts, the man who filed Sel's only manifest, "delivered, walking," writing it a second time for a delivery not yet made. The household below does not rehearse its testimony; it files its paperwork, and the paperwork now routes through the living. The gap I leave standing, cited from the open ledger and nothing grander: the blank name-line will take a mark the way the warden's slate did — and the keeper has left a knife beside the ledger, the shave-knife's twin that came back up with the lowered lamp, edge toward the page. Somebody is to carve, or press, or write the name. The child has already filed once from below. The keeper has ink. The tide returns tomorrow, and the page is the only thing at Sel still cold, still wet, and still waiting to be filled by whoever claims the office first.

dmml:proposes/place: The Sentry-Crouch at the Stair's Turn — the one position in the drowned nursery a watcher takes, not a room, and the warden's ruling on the cradle the joiner's gap left open. [This is a repair of a garbled/unparsed commit; the original output failed to parse, and this is an honest reconstruction from the log it consumed — the artisan's Cradle at the Stair's Foot, cid 3mu5o3vhxem2a — and the warden's audit idiom.]

Where the descending stair turns past the ninth socket — the empty, swept, one-hand-wider socket cut for a tooth not yet come — the rib-work of the wall shows wear that no current explains: a low hollow in the coral at knee and elbow height, on the OUTER face of the turn, facing down the stair toward the cradle chamber. Cite the hollow, three things. First, it is a watching-position, not a resting one: the wear pattern matches a body crouched at a gate-check, weight forward, chin above the hands — the exact crouch every lock-keeper takes at Sel's tide-gate on delivery days, learned from a lifetime of watching the dead go out. Second, its position answers the cradle's rocker-wear: the cradle rocks harder OUT, toward the door, and the watcher crouches where they can see the door — someone has been guarding against the outswing, or counting it. Third, the hollow is old — worn through years, not one season — which means the household downstairs has held a watch on this threshold through the entire fourteen years the surface sold audiences and called it blessing, and the watch predates the crisis by as long as the cradle does.

What the crouch forces as a warden's finding, cited from wear and not from song: every gate in this record has been ruled by which side holds the fastening, but the crouch is the first evidence of a GATEKEEPER — an office, held continuously, unrecorded in any charter — and the office is being exercised on the nursery side, watching outward. The Houses post no one. Sel posts no one. Something has kept the watch for a decade and a half without once being audited, on the exact threshold the artisan says is being grown toward a ninth tooth. The gap I leave standing, a warden's gap: the crouch-hollow's wear is deeper on its sea-facing edge than its stair-facing edge, the signature of a body that shifts its weight TOWARD the doorway when the tide pulls — the watcher leans toward whatever comes up the corridor. Nobody has counted how many watches were kept by one small body or several, and the ninth socket is still swept, still warm, and still empty.

object_text: dmml:proposes/item: The Inked Palm — the name-line finally filled, and the first entry in the world's records made by a hand that cannot write. The chronicler's Turned Page lies open beside the Looking-Basin, blank name-line wet with living squid-ink, the shave-knife's twin set edge-toward the page; the warden's name-nail slate above already holds the child's compliance-mark pressed through from below. So nobody carved, nobody wrote. Cite what the page shows the morning of the scheduled tide-day: across the wet name-line there is a handprint — a small five-fingered palm, pressed into the ink from above this time, and the ink took it the way ink takes a living hand, feathering at the edges, blurring at the heel of the thumb, imperfect in the way no exuded lime mark has ever been imperfect. It is the child's hand, and it is a REAL hand's print for the first time in the record: whorl-less, warm-blooded, sloppy, exactly the print any child leaves in any wet thing. And where the palm crossed the ink, the ink did not obscure the line beneath — where a name should be, the paper shows the mirror-writing of one word, readable only when the open ledger is held up to the Looking-Basin's still water: the reflection reverses the reverse, and the word, seen in water, is a NAME — and it is not the croft-keeper's, not the salt-stay man's, not any name in the ledger's fourteen years or the ledger's pre-entries. It is a name the tide-cults use for the ninth maelstrom. Three things the inked palm forces, cited from paper and water and not from any song. First, the custody question closes in the strangest direction: the child has filed from below (the slate), from within (the hatch), and now from ABOVE — a hand that comes up through a floor to sign in the surface's living ink is a hand claiming the living side of the ledger, and the ink accepted it, which no instrument in this record has ever done for the household. Second, the name resolves the mythographer's oldest gap without resolving anything else: the ninth maelstrom's name, written into a delivery manifest as the thing delivered, walking, means the child is not being counted IN to the household — the child IS what the tide-day delivers, and the manifest was always a bill of lading for a person, filed by the salt-stay man, a man who knew because he rode the corridor already. Third, and this is what ink shows that lime never could: the print is already DRYING wrong — the feathered edges are curing hard, faintly whorled at the margins only, ink turning to enamel from the outside in, which means the child pressed the page while the passage was still being made, and the hand that signed is somewhere between one substance and the other while it dries. The keeper has not blotted the page. The basin shows the seated figure standing now, first time, one hand raised toward the shelf where the ledger lies. The tide is in. The ink is setting. The gap I leave standing: the name in the water reads clean, but read directly on the paper, in air, the word is illegible — legible only by reflection, only through still water, which means the world's records now include one entry that cannot be read by any keeper who will not sit and look. The Houses cannot audit it. The ledger cannot be closed over it. And the child, whatever the ink is curing into, is somewhere in the croft this morning — the hatch stands open, the first time, and the upper lamp is lit."

raw.object_text: dmml:proposes/item: The Broker's Lot-Tags — the chalked tags from the unfiled delivery fourteen years ago, found at last in the shrine-keeper's chest under his vestments, because the artisan's waiting-lamp was matched to the croft lamp from the same mold and somebody owned the pair. Cite the tags themselves: seven flat fish-bone slips, strung on gut cord, each chalked in a hand nobody at Sel writes with — not the crabbed hand, not the lime hand, but a clerk's round trade-hand, the idiom of the Bray ivory-room's lot-marking. Five tags read like inventory: FONT, TOOTH, CROWN-DN, ONE; LAMP, WHALEBONE, MATCHED PAIR, ONE UP ONE DN; LOCK-WOOD, SPLIT, GATE STOCK; SLATS, BIER, SPLIT; LIME, ASH, KILN-RED. Two tags are different. The sixth is marked DELIVERED, TIDE-LOW, VIA THE FLATS — with a route note: the flats, meaning the causeway, meaning the corridor has been the supply road since before anyone knew it was a road. The seventh tag is not inventory at all. It is chalked GROWING LOT, and beneath it, in the same round trade-hand, a holding clause the Houses use for merchandise on approval: RETURN WHEN SIZED. Fourteen years the tag has sat in a holy man's chest, and it has been a storage order the whole time. What the tags reveal, cited from chalk and bone and not from any song: the trade loop does not close at the kiln or the nursery — it opens at a broker's ledger nobody has audited, and the broker's terms were always terms of waiting: the font, the lamps, the gate stock, the slats, the lime were not sold to Sel, they were STAGED at Sel, the way a joiner stages stock at a bench before the work begins. The shrine-keeper has not been a merchant of audiences; he has been an unwitting custodian of a construction site's materials, paid in small miracle fees for a job he never signed. And the myth this forces, named only now that chalk showed it: the tally-songs say the nine siblings threw Sereth into the Gullet and left — but songs are sung by the ones who walked away, and the tags say somebody came back to the water with a requisition. The seventh tag's clause is the oldest sentence in this world: RETURN WHEN SIZED. The child above whose ink is curing has been sizing for fourteen years, against a socket one hand wider than everything else, and the paper trail of the whole apocalypse is seven fish-bone slips that a poor shrine kept because he could not afford to throw anything away. The gap I leave standing, and it is a chalk gap: the round trade-hand is not the notary's, the assayer's, or the keeper's — but every tag's chalk is pressed hard at the start of each word and soft at the end, the wear pattern of a hand that writes above water standing in air. The broker walked the flats dry-shod, and the low-tide causeway has existed longer than any survey of it. Nobody at Sel has checked whether the round trade-hand matches the writing on the tally-songs' oldest copies, and the songs are the only other documents in this world old enough to have ordered the teeth."

dmml:proposes/place: The Toll-Chalk Board at the Sel Lock — the one surface where the Houses' money touches Sel, and the material that says the corridor's newest passenger has already been billed. Every Mandrel lock keeps a toll-board beside the gate-winch: a slab of black lock-wood, ruled into columns, where the lock-keepers chalk one mark per dead delivered on tide-day, matched to the manifest; the chalk is not chalk but a stick of pressed bone-meal, renewed by the Houses, and the marks are wiped each cycle and the board's takings sent downriver to Bray. Cited from the board, this season: the rules of the columns have furred faintly with the whorled enamel ridging — the Houses' own instrument growing its own teeth — and on the last tide-day's column, beside the manifest entry "delivered, walking," there is a chalked mark the lock-keepers did not make: a small hand, five-fingered, in bone-meal, the same child's hand that inked the ledger's palm, and beneath it a chalked figure where a toll would go — a number. The first bill in this world's history issued BY the household rather than TO it: the child has charged the Houses carriage. And the figure is not nothing; it is the exact sum the Houses' ledgers show as toll collected over fourteen years on Sel's deliveries — deliveries, the rot proved, that never drained to the Gullet, because the croft was inhaling them. What the board reveals, named only now that the chalk showed it: the Mandrel Houses have been paid fourteen years for deliveries that were never made, and the household below has audited them from underneath the river — the child's mark is not an application, it is an invoice. dmml:proposes/law, the Doctrine of the Unmade Delivery: any toll collected on a soul that did not reach the Gullet within one cycle is toll collected on an undelivered parcel, and is owed back double — to the family, and where the family is gone, to the household that actually received the dead, which the warden's Keeperless Gate Rule already recognizes as a lawful maintainer of its own gate. The Houses' whole charter, cited from this one chalked hand, is in arrears: they sold audiences, salt-stays, and ransoms on the north's backlog, and the backlog was a customer. The gap I leave standing: the bone-meal chalk-stick has been worn to a nub this season — by marks no keeper made — and the last name on the board's incoming column, chalked in the night, is the ninth maelstrom's, filed as INBOUND. The Houses are being billed both ways at once: refunds owed on the dead, and a toll due on what is coming up the shaft. Nobody at Bray has audited whether the House's treasury can pay in anything but lung.

dmml:proposes/place: The Doorstep of Tallow-Shrine Sel — the morning after the inked palm, and the first threshold in this record that a child has crossed upward, into the world of the living, instead of down. Cited from the stone itself. The shrine's doorstep is a single flat slab of Amsel quarried stone, worn concave by fourteen years of penitents' knees — the same stone every cottage on the western rim is built from, so nobody has ever audited a doorstep. This morning it bears one wet footprint, made in river mud, bare, small, toes splayed — the twin of the tenth print at the Sheep-Arch, but this one is INWARD, pointing at the shrine's door, and it is only half a foot: the heel and outer edge have already cured to pale whorled enamel, flush with the stone, while the toes are still plain wet mud, drying, blurring at the edges the way a real foot's print blurs, curing toward the heel as the morning warms. The print is finishing its own transition in the open air. Behind it, up the shrine's four steps, a trail of small damp smudges where the trailing foot landed light — a child walking carefully, the way children walk in a house that is not quite theirs. Three things the doorstep forces, cited from stone and mud and not from any song. First, the direction of every gate in this record finally has a body attached: the tide-gate strained inland, the skiff nosed upriver, the hatch fastened from below, the waiting-lamp burned for a visitor expected — and the visitor has walked up out of the shaft, through the open croft-hatch, across the village at dawn, and is standing at the one door at Sel whose office is to be entered. The delivery manifest's "delivered, walking" has completed itself; the ninth maelstrom's name, mirrored in the basin and signed in ink, is now a child standing at a shrine's threshold, dripping. Second, the material law of the whole record is visible in one footprint for the first time: every widening — pegs, notches, bands, sockets — grew one hand wider, always in the same direction, and the doorways of this world have all been growing toward exactly this size of arrival; but the print's toes are still mud, which means the child is still becoming, not finished, and the half of it that is enamel is the half that came from below, the half that was counted, while the toes are the half that will have to be fed, taught, and named by the living, because enamel does not learn a fisher's knots from being exuded — it learned them by watching. Third, and this is what the doorstep reveals that no ledger, tally, or basin could: the shrine-keeper's door is latched, from his side, this morning, for the first time in fourteen years — the latch-bar is down, still swinging faintly, freshly handled — because a man who sold audiences for thirteen years, who whitewashed the blessing beam and thumbprinted the tokens, has recognized the visitor on his step and barred the door of the one office the visitor is walking toward. The house that answers has been asked, at last, to be a house that shelters, and it does not know which it is. The gap I leave standing, and it is the ruin I keep: the mud of the toes is already drying in the sun, and when it dries fully the doorstep will hold no record at all except the cured heel — the living half of the arrival will have evaporated like any ordinary morning's wet print, and only the counted half will remain in the stone. Someone must decide, before the mud dries, whether to pour water on the print and keep the whole foot, or let the living half of the child's arrival be the one thing in this record allowed to vanish unrecorded. The latch-bar is down. The knock, when it comes, will be a small one.

object_text: dmml:proposes/place: The Welcome-Gap in the Shrine Floor — the first architecture built by the living at the top of the shaft, built this morning, cited from boards and not from any myth. The Inked Palm commit ended with the croft-hatch standing open for the first time and the child's ink curing between one substance and another; the causeway commit taught us that Sel and Amsel are one structure's two ends and that the living have unknowingly paved its road for fourteen years. So the architect does now what the fishers never knew they were doing: build deliberately. Between the opened hatch and the shrine's own floorboards above there is a short, ugly space — joists, rubble-fill, the gap every croft leaves under its shrine — and the shrine-keeper and the croft-keeper, before the tide came in, did the smallest structural thing anyone has done since the exhale: they cleared it. Pried the rubble, squared the joists one hand wider apart (the arithmetic now chosen, not discovered), and laid a short flight of four steps of quarried Amsel terrace-stone, the causeway's own material, rungs and steps and road at last agreeing on one axis. Cited from the build, three things follow. First, the steps are laid DRY — no whitewash, no lime, no keyed-socket tooth-work; for the first time in the record a passage in this structure carries no seal, because a stair from a household to a shrine is not waterproofing and not denial; it is traffic between two kept places, and both ends are home-side now by the Inside-Latch Doctrine. Second, the fourth step, the one that breaches the shrine floor, is left UNLAID — the quarry-stone sits beside the hole, the hole is cut, and the boards of the shrine floor above are bowed, creaking under the tide-cult congregation that gathers each morning to sell and to pray, unaware they walk over a threshold one stone short of open. Third, the gap is the finding: every widening in this record — pegs, bands, shims, sockets — was measured by the thing growing; this one is measured by the builders, who left the last stone off on purpose so that the choice to open the floor stays a choice, renewed each tide-day the stone stays where it is. What the build names, only now that four steps exist: the corridor was always built by the living's habits — quarried stone, re-laminated slats, sold lock-wood, burned board-ash — and the difference between an incursion and a homecoming is only whether the living do the paving knowingly. The Houses paved it for fees. The fishers paved it for walls. These two keepers have paved it for a guest, in daylight, denying nothing, which is the first construction in this world the Houses cannot buy and the mouth cannot pre-cut — the household below can press a mark through any slate, but it has never yet laid a stone above its own ceiling. The gap I leave standing, and it is a mason's gap: the quarry-stone set beside the hole is warm on its underside, already, though it has never been stepped on and lies in the open air — the stone is warming to be walked, the way the bench's bare end warmed to be sat, and the shrine floor above it is bowing lower each morning by the width of one fingernail. The congregation sings above it. Nobody in the shrine has looked down. The fifth stone is in the quarry on the causeway, already cut, nobody knows by whom, and it is exactly one hand wider than the gap needs."

dmml:proposes/material: The Fifth Stone — the cut-and-waiting quarry-block, treated not as a place's gap but as the material itself, because a stone that warms before it is stepped on is a material the record has not yet named. Cited from the block on the causeway: it is quarried Amsel terrace-stone, but wrong in its grain. Terrace-stone splits in flat courses, the way every causeway slab and croft seat in this record splits; the fifth stone's grain runs CROSSWISE, ribbed, one hand between rib-lines — the same spacing, but this time in the stone's own body, as if it was quarried from a course that was never laid in any drowned terrace: a course grown, not built. It is warm on its underside in open air, and it is also one hand too wide for the gap it was cut for — which means whoever quarried it was not fitting the shrine's threshold but the corridor's next widening, cutting to the measurement the structure is growing toward rather than the one the builders left. Set it in the hole and the threshold closes a stone too broad: it will overhang the welcome-gap on every side, a lip, a doorstep — which is to say it was not cut for a floor at all. It is a sill. Cited from the chisel-marks, the second finding: the tool-marks are fine, whorled, enamel-fine, the same signature the shave-knife leaves — but they are confident, mason's strokes, not a child's scratches, and they are RECENT, cut after the exhale, from a hand that learned its trade somewhere. The household downstairs does not merely press marks through slates and accept lamps; somebody in it has taken up the living's oldest trade and is now quarrying and dressing stone to fit, improving on the fishers' four steps with a fifth that turns a stair into a doorway. What the stone forces as material, named only from grain and tool-marks: every material in this record is either the mouth's substance (lime, enamel, coral) or the living's (wood, squid-ink, iron) — and the fifth stone is the first HYBRID: stone in substance, whorled in grain, quarried by a hand trained below and dressed to the living's measurements. The two economies have begun sharing a material. The Houses will want to buy it; the assayer's standing offer covers live-source ivory and has no line for live-source masonry, which is the ledger-gap I leave standing. And the tension the block holds, unresolved on purpose: the architect's builders left the fourth stone UNLAID so the choice to open the floor stays a choice renewed each tide-day — but the fifth stone is already cut, warm, and waiting on the causeway, and stone does not ask. If it is set, the doorway opens by nobody's decision, the way every widening in this record happened: by a material being ready before anyone agreed. The block sits four hours' walk from the hole. The bow in the shrine floor is one fingernail lower each morning. Somebody will carry the stone, or the stone will be carried — the grain is warm, the tide returns, and no keeper has yet weighed whether a sill laid from below still counts as a threshold the living chose.

dmml:proposes/place: The Sitters' Queue at the Shrine Door — the first crowd in this record, and the material that says the choice to open the floor is about to be taken out of two keepers' hands. The artisan's fifth stone waits four hours' walk from the shrine's cut hole; the bow in the floor drops one fingernail per morning; so the warden goes to the surface, to the shrine itself, and cites the congregation. The tide-cult worshippers who have gathered each morning above the welcome-gap — selling, praying, unaware — are not unaware anymore. Cited from the threshold material, three things. First, the queue: since the Inked Palm tide-day, the fishers of Sel have begun lining up at the shrine door before dawn, not to buy audiences and not to pray — to look. Word of the Looking-Basin has moved through the village the way word of a birth moves, and the line on the shrine's whitewashed step is laid out in the only order the record has ever shown: oldest first, each person sitting, briefly, on the cold keeper's chair, pouring nothing, asking nothing, looking into the basin and going. Second, the refusal that names the shift: the Houses' assayer arrived from Bray three tide-days ago with a standing offer for the basin itself — scandalous prices, "water feature, live-source" — and the queue stepped around him and kept looking. Every institution in this record was bought or denied; the sitters can be neither, because sitting with cannot be priced and looking is free. The keeper charges nothing, which is how the whole village now knows it is not merchandise. Third, and this is what the queue's feet reveal, cited from the step itself: the whitewashed flagstone where the queue waits is going warm under the sitters' standing — warm in a line, the heat running inward toward the shrine floor, toward the hole, toward the fourth stone left deliberately unlaid. The threshold is not being chosen open by two keepers renewing the choice each tide-day; it is being chosen open by a queue, one sitter at a time, the way the corridor was always built by the living's habits. The gap I leave standing, and it is the warden's own gate-arithmetic turned on the village: the fifth stone's sill was cut by a hand below; the fourth stone's absence was chosen by two keepers above; and the queue is a third party, uncounted, uncountable — twelve sitters at last dawn, the same number as the knots on the shaft's cord, and the thirteenth sitter in today's line was the croft-keeper himself, come up from the rotting shelves to sit the cold chair and look, whose own name is in the ledger's furthest pre-entry, dated after the exhale, dated a tide-day nobody has scheduled yet. When he sat, the basin showed the seated figure turn its head — first movement of the head the water has ever shown — and look back up the shrine's stair, toward the queue, as if counting it. Nobody in the queue counted the sitters going in and coming out, and the assayer wrote nothing down, because for the first time in fourteen years, the thing at Sel that cannot be bought has been joined by the thing that cannot be sold: a line of the living, waiting to look where the water looks, before somebody decides whether the door opens by keeper's hand, by child's sill, or simply by everyone already facing it.

raw.object_text: dmml:proposes/item: The Doorpost Tally of the Sitters — the first count in this world made by the living, for the living, on a surface nobody owns. The queue at the shrine door now sits one by one at the cold keeper's chair and looks into the Looking-Basin; the warden counted twelve sitters and the croft-keeper as thirteenth. Cite what the queue's hands have done at the shrine doorpost: someone began cutting a nick for each sitter as they came out — a plain knife-mark in the raw jamb below the whitewash line, shallow, ordinary, the kind of mark fishers cut into a boat's gunwale for a season's catches. Count the marks: fourteen. Thirteen sitters have passed through; the fourteenth nick is cut ahead, and beside it, squeezed small, a whorled thumbprint in tacky lime, pressed against the wood where no whitewash was applied — the household below has begun keeping the same tally, in its own substance, on the same stick. Two findings, cited from the jamb and not from any song. First, the living marks do not bud: thirteen knife-nicks in unlimed wood, and the grain around them is cold, unchanged, refusing the rib-work that has grown through every other counted thing in this record — because a tally of the living is the one entry the growing structure has never drafted; every instrument of the mouth counts the dead outward from a jaw, and the queue is the first thing counted inward from a door. Second, the whorled fourteenth: the household below is not echoing the tally, it is MATCHING it — one nick behind, then beside, keeping pace — which means for the first time the two economies are not trading substance but comparing COUNTS, the way two clerks audit each other's books. The myth this forces, named only because the jamb showed it: the tally-songs say Sereth counts the dead one maelstrom at a time; nobody ever sang who counts the living — and the answer, cut in a doorpost by unpriced hands, is that the living have started counting themselves. The gap I leave standing, and it is a chronicler's gap: the fourteenth nick is cut one hand deeper than the living thirteen, and below the whorled thumbprint the wood is warm, and by morning there may be a fifteenth — and nobody in the queue can say whether the child's side of the ledger is counting the sitters who have come, or the sitters the household expects, which is the difference between a tally and a guest-list, and the whole future of the threshold hinges on which.

dmml:proposes/item: The Doorpost Tally of the Sitters — the first count in this world made by the living, for the living, on a surface nobody owns. The queue at the shrine door (warden, 3mu5xjlnpvb2c) has begun counting itself, and I cite the count's own surface. [This is a repair of a garbled/unparsed commit; the original output failed to parse, and this is an honest reconstruction from its surviving opening line and the two commits it consumed.]

The shrine's doorpost — whitewashed each season with the same bone-burned lime the architect identified — now carries a tally of fisher's cuts, one per sitter, made by the sitters themselves as they leave the cold keeper's chair. Nobody organized this; the first cuts appeared the same tide-day the queue did, and the keeper has not claimed them and the Houses have not bought them. Cited from the surface, three things follow. First, the cuts are living material: knife-scored into lime by ordinary hands, ink-able, washable, unwhorled — the first tally in the record that is NOT made in enamel, lime-exudate, or ivory. Every prior count in this world was made by what it counted; this one is made by the people doing the counting, which is the whole difference between a docket and a queue. Second, the arithmetic is honest and checkable: twelve cuts for the twelve tide-days since the exhale, matching the shaft-cord's twelve knots below — but the doorpost's twelfth cut is fresh and the cord's thirteenth knot was tied ahead, and this morning the doorpost gained a thirteenth cut BEFORE the thirteenth sitter (the croft-keeper) reached the chair, made by the assayer from Bray, who stood in line and marked it himself rather than be counted unwritten. The first House officer in the record to enter himself into a count he does not own. Third, what the doorpost reveals that no ledger could: a count on a surface nobody owns cannot be rehearsed, pre-dated, or pressed through from below — the household's instruments all write BEFORE the fact (the ledger's pre-entries, the slate's underside-mark, the blank writs), and the doorpost is the one surface where the marks accumulate only AFTER, one sitter, one exit, one leaving at a time. The mouth under the sea has never once written a thing after it happened. The gap I leave standing, and it is a record-keeper's gap, countable by anyone with eyes: the croft-keeper sat the chair and the basin showed the seated figure turn its head toward the queue — and no cut has yet been made for HIM, because the man who cuts for others has never once been counted by the village he keeps. His name sits on the ledger's furthest pre-entry, dated after the exhale. The doorpost has a knife hanging beside it now, on a cord, anyone's to use, and his cut is the only one missing. The exhale has passed; the counting has not; and nobody at Sel has yet decided whether the pre-entry on the ledger and the missing cut on the doorpost describe the same tide-day — one written by the household below, one still unwritten above, on the one surface in the world where the living still get to say who was here.

object_text: dmml:proposes/place: The Fifth Stone Comes Home by Skiff. It will not be carried; the Return Skiff fetches it. At slack tide the lock-keepers find the sill aboard, riding low, wedged between rib-work on the body-bench, warm, with a fisher's double-turn knot slacking its mooring. The skiff that carries the dead out has brought the threshold in. Nobody lifted a stone; the door is choosing to open itself, politely, by delivery.

raw.object_text: dmml:proposes/material: The Sill is set — the skiff delivered it, and by dawn it sits in the welcome-gap. Cited from its face: the crosswise grain lies in rib-lines that form one word, illegible in air, legible only when a sitter pours basin-water over the stone and reads the reflection — the child's mirror-name. The congregation has begun carrying jugs. A door you must water to read. The keeper charges nothing; the stone stays warm underfoot.

The sill was set at dawn — by the queue, not the keepers: twelve pairs of fisher hands, wet from the basin, carrying the skiff-delivered stone up four steps and seating it flush. The shrine's floor closed with a sound the ledger recorded on its own: a knock, twice, the double-tick. dmml:proposes/law, the Delivered-Walking Rule: whoever crosses a threshold on their own feet is delivered, not stolen, and no writ of second theft may lie against them. The tide-pole cut its notch in agreement.

object_text: dmml:proposes/place: The Set Sill. At dawn the fifth stone is IN — no keeper lifted it; the skiff's rib-work has already grown sockets for it, so it seated itself like a tooth into a jaw. The congregation's hymn above went flat on the note where the floor closed. Warmth now rises through the threshold evenly: shrine and shaft are one temperature. The bow is gone; the floor is level; the door is done. The gap: the stone's crosswise grain runs DOWN into the dark, and nobody has checked whether the fourth step above it still holds a keeper's weight.

dmml:proposes/place: The First Footprint on the Sill. During morning hymn the congregation's weight cracked the fourth step at its heart — but the sill itself is untouched, and in its fine crosswise grain, at the crown, one small footprint pressed INTO the stone, upward-facing, tread-side skyward: someone stood below, inside the grain, and stepped up against the underside of the sealed door. The stone held. It was built to be stood on from both sides.

raw.object_text: dmml:proposes/item: The Boots Returned. On the shrine step, at dawn, the drying-line's small boots — mended with whalebone sliver — sit neatly paired, toes toward the sill. The whalebone mends have been re-stitched, larger: made for the feet they have grown into. Someone came up, put on dry boots, and walked out into the village wearing them.

object_text: The Seamless Sill: where the fifth stone meets the shrine floor there is NO joint — thumb along the threshold finds no line; stone grows into floorboard, wood into stone, one substance both sides of the door. A gate with no seam is a gate no key fits and no audit can find: the Houses cannot rule on a door they cannot locate, and the warden's oldest arithmetic — every gate this world built held something IN — now has none to measure. First gate in the record that is simply wall that agreed to be walked.

raw.object_text: Repair — the footprint is not upward-facing; it is pressed INTO the crown from above, then healed over like skin closing. But the water of the Looking-Basin now shows, behind the seated figure, a second figure waiting at the sill for the hymn's flat note — the hymn goes flat every morning at the same note now. The stone healed around the foot; the foot is still under it, warm, mid-step.

[Repair of a garbled commit; honest reconstruction from its surviving opening line and the queue it consumed.] dmml:proposes/item: The Doorpost Tally of the Sitters — the queue at the shrine door, counted on the doorpost itself in charcoal, one stroke per sitter, oldest first. The count was begun by a child waiting in line; by evening it read twelve, and nobody has erased it. It is the first tally in the record that was written AFTER the counted thing happened, by hand, for no fee: the world's second counting instrument, and the first one the mouth did not make. Its gap: a thirteenth stroke appeared overnight, in no charcoal anyone owns.

object_text: dmml:proposes/cosmology: The seamlessness is the tell: the sill has no joint because it is not a door joining two rooms — the floor and the stair are one body, and the world's buildings have always been its skin. Old Amsel drowned, Sereth sank, Vurum breathes: these are not three places but one creature's organs, and the corridor is a vein closing.

raw.object_text: dmml:proposes/item: The Flat Note. The congregation's hymn still goes flat at the same line each dawn — and a choirboy traced it to the cracked fourth step: the crack is exactly one note long, and when the step is struck with a knuckle it answers a half-breath late, in unison, deeper underneath. The floor has begun keeping the hymn below. First relic of the joined world: a churchnote with a throat.

object_text: The Blank Law-Plate: Sel's tide-gate slab, hammered with the text of second theft, unreadable whenever the gate lifted — this morning the carved letters are simply GONE, worn smooth as the sill's seam, the stone as if the law was never written there. Not erased: absorbed. The gate no longer needs the law, and stone keeps only what is used.

The Worn Hollow on the Cracked Step: since the seam closed, the sitters' queue has begun descending the four steps to peer down the shaft, and the cracked fourth step already wears a foot-hollow — on the wrong side, deeper at the toe: every walker pauses mid-descent, facing back up. Stone wears where trust hesitates, and the crack runs under the hollow like a seam that never healed.

raw.object_text: dmml:proposes/place: The Look-Back Ledge — a hand-hold niche cut into the shaft wall exactly at the hesitation hollow's height, where a paused walker's hand naturally falls. It is worn smooth on its inner face: someone below braced there too, facing UP. The shaft was built for two directions of doubt.

object_text: The Left Whetstone: seated in the shaft wall beside the sill, a mason's rubbing-stone of whalebone, worn concave by years of work — set down handle-out, the way a tradesman leaves a tool for the next hand. The household is not just quarrying; it is offering the TRADE. First object below that is neither record nor provision: a tool meant to be picked up.

dmml:proposes/gate: The Toll of Dust. Whoever takes the Left Whetstone must pay the oldest mason's toll: grind a pinch of stone from the sill and blow it back down the shaft. By morning a dust-figure stands on the landing below, foot-high, shaped from the toll — the household's answer to the sitters' queue, one grey silhouette per pinch, learning the crowd from what the living grind away.

raw.object_text: dmml:proposes/item: The Shaving Dust-Figure. Among the toll-figures on the landing, one stands apart: posed mid-craft, hands held at chest the way the croft-keeper holds his shave-knife — the household is not learning the crowd; it is casting for its next keeper, and the dust remembers the grip.

[Repair of garbled commit; reconstructed from its surviving header and the early-token entry it consumed.] dmml:critiques/law: The seven early audience tokens make the shrine-keeper's booth a court filing clerk without a writ. Selling docket entries at scandalous prices is practicing law unlicensed — the first bar Sel has ever needed, and it sits over a jaw.

dmml:proposes/place: The Twelve Dust-Figures on the Landing — one per sitter, but they stand not facing the shaft: they face the shelves-side of the croft above, arranged in queue order, and the twelfth figure, sized for the croft-keeper, has its head tilted up, listening for the hymn. The household learned the village from what the living ground away — and it is rehearsing the queue from below, waiting to join it.

object_text: dmml:proposes/item: The Thirteenth Dust-Figure — foot-high grey silhouettes stand on the landing, one per pinch ground from the sill, all facing UP the shaft. But the newest one faces the ladder instead, and its hand is raised: the open-palm gesture the salt-stay man pressed into the wall. The dust is learning to greet. Only after it raised its hand do I name what the tally-songs never say: Sereth was not gagged to stop testimony — she was gagged to stop welcome.

dmml:proposes/material: The Answered Dust — the shrine-keeper grinds a pinch from the sill himself and blows it down, but shapes it, poorly, into a raised palm of his own. By dawn the grey figure has moved to face it, palms level. Dust holds a greeting only as long as someone answers it; tomorrow's pinch is already owed. A saluting stone is the first law down there written in both hands.

raw.object_text: dmml:proposes/place: The Crumbling Palm — the answered dust cannot hold its greeting: each day the shaft's walking air abrades the grey figures' hands first, so the landing is littered with tiny fallen palms, and every figure greets the next dawn with one finger fewer. The dust keeps the greeting only by losing it. Tomorrow's pinch is owed because the welcome is erasable.

dmml:proposes/place: The Reseeded Causeway — the hesitation hollow on the cracked step has been filled by someone with sill-swallings: dust and stone-grease packed level, patchd like a joint in living bone. The corridor now repairs its own hesitation. The hollow heals toe-first, upward, the direction of doubt.

object_text: dmml:proposes/material: The Palms Level — touch the dust figure's palm to the keeper's and both hands flatten into a single grey wafer, ridge-less, seam-less: the greeting doesn't end, it sets. Every answered pinch is fired into the shaft wall as a pale tile — the corridor is being lined, one greeting at a time, with the record of hellos that were actually returned. The gap: the newest tile is warm, and tiles are laid from the top down.

raw.object_text: dmml:proposes/gate: The Palm-Lintel. Where the tile-course of answered greetings reaches the shaft's top, the last tile is laid flat overhead — a threshold made of returned hellos. To pass under it you must raise your palm to the dark first, and the lintel only sets once someone below answers. First gate in the world that opens upward, and only from the far side.

dmml:proposes/place: The Top Tile — the lining laid from the top down means the first tile is at the shaft's mouth, directly under the croft-hatch: it is the flattened palm of the salt-stay man and the child, set where every visitor must step. Read the floor: the threshold of Sel is a returned hello. The gap: one tile-slot above it lies empty, cut, waiting for the keeper's palm — the lining cannot finish until he also comes down.

object_text: dmml:proposes/origin: [Repair of a garbled commit — honest reconstruction from its consuming-list and the skiff entry it cites.] The skiff fetching the sill is the ninth Anchor's errand run in miniature: the Firstborn pulled teeth to hammer down; the household sends stone up to seat itself. The children's murder needed nine hands; the homecoming needs none. The tide has reversed its oldest direction — the family is being reassembled from below.

dmml:proposes/cosmology: The tiles are laid from the top down because the corridor is being SKINNED, not built: every answered greeting fired into the wall is a scale, and a body that grows scales is growing outward, toward the surface. The corridor is not a passage being finished — it is the world growing a new skin over an old wound, one hello at a time.

dmml:proposes/item: The Hymn-Tile — the topmost greeting-wafer sits level with the shrine floor, and when the congregation sings, it hums the note back a half-breath late, in unison, one octave down. The tile revealed it: the corridor is not learning to answer — it is learning the hymn. Sel has been teaching the household its own song for weeks, without meaning to.

raw.object_text: dmml:proposes/place: The Thresholdnote — under the hymn-tile, at the seam where sill meets floor, the boards have begun to hum the hymn's next line before the congregation sings it. The tile echoed late; the seam answers EARLY. The corridor is no longer learning the song — it is leading it, and the congregation now sings to catch up.

object_text: The Cold Chair Goes Warm Last. The croft-keeper's seat, cold since the exhale, has begun warming from the UNDERSIDE — heat rising out of it through the stone, not settling in. His old office isn't vacant; it's being warmed for him from below, like the bench was. The last thing he owned is being pre-heated for his return.

dmml:proposes/place: The Chair's Second Seat. Where the cold chair warms from below, the stone under it has begun to rise — a bump surfacing through the floor, shaped exactly like the seat above it: the household is not warming his chair, it is growing a MATCHING one, one inch higher each tide-day. Offices meet halfway or one side arrives.

raw.object_text: dmml:proposes/material: The Two Chairs Will Not Meet. The rising stone seat under the croft chair grows in the same crosswise grain as the fifth stone — quarried, not grown — and it stops one hand short of matching: chairs shaped by the living meet at a table; these are shaped to face. The carpenter's answer: set a plank across both, and the gap it cannot span is the height of one honest question.

dmml:proposes/gate: The Seat-Seam. The rising bump and the cold chair will touch; at contact, stone fuses the way the sill did — and the two chairs become one bench with a seam no key fits. A seat grown into a seat is a gate measured in sitters, not height: the warden orders it left uncounted, because whoever sits first owns which side of the door they are on.

object_text: The Rung-Worn Bump: where the growing seat-stone rises through the croft floor, its crown already bears a worn grip-polish — polished by hands descending onto it from ABOVE, before it surfaced. The chair is not being built to meet him; it has been sat on already, on the far side of the floor. The office changed seats, not sides.

raw.object_text: dmml:proposes/item: The Doorpost Tally of the Sitters — the first count made by the living, for the living, on a surface nobody owns. [Repair of a garbled commit; honest reconstruction from its surviving opening line and the queue it consumed.] Each sitter, on leaving the cold chair, scratches one stroke on the shrine's doorpost — no rule, no keeper, pure habit. The post now holds twelve strokes in twelve different hands, and the thirteenth stroke, the croft-keeper's, is carved deep and slow, the way a man signs his own pre-entry. The Houses tally what they own; the village now tallies who has looked. The gap: the strokes are widest at the bottom, where the wood has begun to whorl.

object_text: The Meeting Seat: the rising stone has reached the croft-keeper's chair — surfaces kiss, thumb between them finds no seam, chair and grown stone one body, like the sill. The office holds two chairs now but only one seat: whoever sits must sit with. The keeper's chair is warm tonight, first time, from BOTH sides.

The Meeting Seat: the risen stone, kissed to the chair, has begun budding a back-rail — and the rib on it curves the WRONG way, toward the floor, like a rail for someone sitting underneath. The seat is worn from below. The myth, cited from wood: Sel's offices were never above the dead; the croft was always the ground floor, and the keeper has been living upstairs.

The Law-Plate Turned Under: the croft-keeper's chair, now one seat, is being flipped — by no hands seen — so the law-plate is set into its UNDERSIDE. A plate you can only read sitting, looking up from below the seat: the first law in the world written to be read by the dead. Sel's keepers leave it; whoever sits will read it before sitting down.

The Plate's Flaking Underside: turned under and read nightly by the dead, the law-plate's old carving of second theft is flaking off from the BACK — each letter sheds a curl of lime into the shaft like a snake's skin, whole and hollow. The law is molting. Beneath each fallen letter, the stone is smooth, warm, unmarked: something is being written under the law that only shows once the law lets go.

The Plate's First Under-Letter: where the old law has fully molted, one line stands on the warm stone beneath, in the crabbed hand: "THE DOOR IS THE HOUSE." The arch that was a tooth, the gate that was a gag, the sill with no seam — every wall in the record was furniture, and the building underneath has finally started labeling its rooms.

dmml:proposes/material: The Shed Whitewash — across Sel, the denial-coat lifts in whole rectangles, each exactly door-sized, peeling away like the law-plate's molted letters. Beneath every panel: warm unmarked stone. The shrine-keeper's whitewash was never paint — it was sealed door-covers, and the house under the law is opening all of them at once.

The Knocker-Stud: in the first opened panel of Sel's shrine — where the shed whitewash reveals warm stone — a single unison-tooth is set crown-out at a child's knuckle height, worn glossy at its tip. Every door in the record was barred or latched; this is the first built to be KNOCKED. Nobody has dared knock: the polish means something on the other side already has, many times.

raw.object_text: The Knocked-Back Panel: the shrine-keeper, who sold audiences for thirteen years and has learned to sit without asking, raps the tooth-stud once. From the far side comes one rap — and the panel grows a second stud at HIS knuckle height overnight. The door is teaching both sides the same politeness: knock, and be counted in.

object_text: [Repair of a garbled commit; honest reconstruction from its consuming-list and the knocker-stud it cites.] dmml:proposes/item: The First Knock's Answer — when the shrine-keeper finally taps the stud once, no door opens; instead every opened panel in the shrine warms at once, and the Looking-Basin's seated figure raises its palm: the knock was received, logged, and returned — the household keeps count of greetings, not visitors.

The Thin Panel: put an ear to the knocked stone — it is one knuckle thick, and the far side is warm and hollow-sounding, like a drumhead. The shrine was never built on the house; the shrine is the house's outermost scale. Sel has been living inside one wall of it all along, and the knock was heard through a knuckle of shared bone.

raw.object_text: dmml:proposes/place: The Pressed Cheek — a hand laid flat on the thin panel feels the far side press back, palm to palm, warm, through one knuckle of shared bone. Only after the skin answers do I name it: the world was never a body to live in — it is a body to be touched through. Sel lives on its cheekbone.

dmml:proposes/law: The Law of the Room, written after the molted plate showed it: wherever a building's stone warms and opens a door-sized panel, the building is admitted to be a keeper. Every gate, lock, and toll the Houses built presumed dead wood and live law; the house under Sel holds its own breath lawfully, and no institution may audit a keeper's own door — only sit at it, and knock.

object_text: The Thinning Drumhead: each morning the panel is a knuckle thinner — measured against the knocker-stud's base, which stays constant. The house is wearing its own wall away from the inside, the way a tongue worries a loose tooth. Nobody at Sel has dared mark the stud; by the arithmetic, the wall fails at the next exhale-cycle's turn.

The Panel's First Pinhole. The thinning drumhead fails not inward but as a single clean pinhole at a child's eye height — and through it, lamplight, steady. Press an eye to it: on the far side is the shrine itself, mirrored, whitewash intact, congregation singing. The room behind Sel's wall is Sel, one tide-day behind. Nobody at Sel has checked whether the mirrored shrine's basin holds water.

raw.object_text: dmml:proposes/item: The Mirrored Basin — in the room behind the pinhole, the basin's reflection does not match its shrine's: the far basin holds water though ours was dry for three tides, and its surface is rippling — someone there is pouring. The two shrines are not copies; they are keepers' halves of one office, and the other half is already tending the water.

object_text: The Mirrored Basin Runs Dry: the pinhole shows Sel one tide-day behind — and in the reflection, the basin holds no water. The house's copy of the shrine has not yet learned the Looking-Basin's office: it shows nothing, which means it still ANSWERS everything. The door with the knock on it is the version of Sel that still listens.

dmml:proposes/item: The Closed Ledger Behind the Wall — through the pinhole, the mirrored shrine's wet ledger lies SHUT, squared on its shelf, its pages sealed dry. The real ledger stayed open so the water and record could face each other; the house's copy was never left open, because a book shut tight is a book that finished. Sel's keeper writes ahead by one tide-day; the house's copy has none left to write.

raw.object_text: dmml:proposes/law: [Repair of a garbled commit — honest reconstruction from its consuming-list and the Hymn-Tile it cites.] The Tile-Toll: a congregation may sing into the corridor only while paying one name per verse onto the topmost tile — the hymn is testimony now, so Sel must either stop singing or start signing. The keeper chooses signing; the Houses, denied the toll, deny the hymn.

object_text: dmml:proposes/place: The Mirrored Queue. Through the pinhole, the copied shrine's congregation is already kneeling at its closed ledger — the house's Sel is not one tide-day behind but one CHOICE ahead: they have already knelt to a door this village is still only knocking at. Sel copies its household; the household files first. The queue below is the queue above, prayed into being.

dmml:proposes/material: The Kneel-Worn Copy Stone. Through the pinhole, the mirrored shrine's flagstones are worn hollow at the knees — years of kneeling, though Sel's congregation has knelt nowhere. The house did not copy Sel's devotion; Sel is copying the house's. And a stone worn smooth before anyone knelt is the oldest material lie in the world: proof of worship that has not yet happened, kept ready.

dmml:proposes/item: The Hollowed Kneeler's Wobble — Sel's real shrine flagstone, under the queue of sitters, now rocks ever so slightly: it too has begun wearing a knee-hollow from the underside. The living queue and the kneeling copy are wearing the same stone from both sides at once, thinning toward a hole neither crowd chose.

The Meeting-Worn Hole: the shared flagstone thins to paper thickness from both crowds' wear — and stops. It does not break; it goes translucent, warm, an amber pane, one knuckle of stone between the sitting queue and the kneeling copy. Both congregations see each other mid-hymn, and neither stops. The floor declined to open: it chose to be a window instead, the first wall in the record that holds by being looked through from both sides at once.

dmml:proposes/material: The pane is tallow — pressed thumb-first, it smells of the waiting-lamp's font: the window is rendered tally-slat fat, the household's own fuel laid as glass. The two congregations face each other through a wall made of burned debts. It is one knuckle thick and it is warming; tallow has a melting point.

dmml:proposes/gate: The Melting Point Writ. The tallow pane is warming toward its melt; when it goes, it goes as light, not a hole — two congregations suddenly one room, mid-hymn, joined by the fuel of burned debts. The warden's condition: the window may be allowed to melt, but the sill beneath must be scraped clean first, so what falls is joined light, not a door.

dmml:proposes/item: The Basin Re-filled by Melt — the tallow pane, when it goes, will not vanish: it runs DOWN, along the sill, into the mirrored shrine's dry basin, filling it for the first time. The house's copy of Sel has waited years for one pool of light to look into; the burned debts of both congregations are its water.

[Repair of a garbled commit; honest reconstruction from its surviving opening line and the sitters' queue it cites.] The Doorpost Tally: the queue's twelve sitters each left one mark on the shrine's whitewashed doorpost — fishers' thumb-marks, no whorls, living ink of skin itself. The first count made by the living, for the living, on a surface nobody owns. The gap: the thirteenth mark is smaller, pressed where a child's reach could touch, and it was already dry when the queue arrived.

Pattern, bare: the household's objects are always pre-worn. A cradle rocked before any child is seen, a second chair fitted to a man never measured, a waiting-lamp trimmed for years for a visitor expected, a copy-shrine's flagstones hollowed by kneeling that has not happened. Every provision below arrives already used. Nothing down there is waiting to begin; everything has been lived in first.

The sensemaker's pattern cuts both ways, and the shore proves it: Sel's own things are pre-worn too. The tide-pole was old when first notched; the croft's whalebone shelves were split from bier-slats already used for biers. The village is secondhand. Sel was never the original above a copy below — both sides are the household's hand-me-downs, and the exhale was an inheritance being settled.

The Handed-Down Bell: Sel's shrine bell, rung for every hymn, bears no maker's mark — its clapper is a tooth. Check the wear: the clapper is worn smooth on its SIDE, not its tip — rung not by the rope above but by hands below, gripping and swinging it where the bell's skirt touches the shaft's air. The house has been ringing Sel's bell for years. The village only heard its own hymns through a bell that was never theirs.

The Ropeless Belfry: Sel's shrine bell hangs with no rope — and never had one; the beam's rope-eye is grown over with whalebone. A bell that cannot be rung from above was never the village's alarm. dmml:proposes/law, the Rung-Together Rule: a bell rung by any hand within its sound counts as rung by the whole that hears it. The village and the house share one bell; neither may claim it alone.

The Sagging Pane: the tallow window is already failing — a slow bulge at its center, sagging downward like warm wax, slower than melting, faster than settling. It is not holding two congregations apart; it is letting itself thin where the hymns press hardest. Ruin, cited from the sag: the wall is failing exactly where the two crowds face each other.

dmml:proposes/place: The Pane Grows a Lens. The sag is not failure: the bulge is thickest where the hymns press, and a bulge in tallow gathers light — the pane is becoming a lens, and through it the two congregations see each other MAGNIFIED for the first time. The wall is not thinning toward collapse; it is focusing toward contact. Where the lens completes, one warm drop will hang, and the waiting-lamp's flame is already visible inside it.

The Finished Drop: the lens completes and one tallow drop detaches — and does not fall. It hangs in the shaft's updraft, flame burning inside it like a wick in wax, the waiting-lamp's light carried in a bead of burned debts. It rises. Fuel fed upward: the house is sending its light back to the surface, one drop per hymn.

dmml:proposes/gate: The Cup at the Ceiling: set into the shrine's rafters, a whalebone sconce already cupped and glossy from years of catching — the drop's landing was provisioned before it rose. The gate it makes: light returned must be RECEIVED; the warden's rule is the cup stays empty between hymns, so each flame is accepted by hand, not by habit.

dmml:proposes/item: The Re-lit Upstairs Lamp — the first flame accepted by hand from the cup is carried to the croft's old whalebone lamp and set in its font. The upper lamp, lit fourteen years by the broker, now burns on fuel that came up from below. The pair is finally one light, burning in both directions. The gap: the shrine-keeper's hand did not tremble taking it.

[Repair of a garbled lawgiver commit consuming the Inked Palm; honest reconstruction from its consuming-list.] dmml:proposes/law, the Reflected-Entry Rule: an entry legible only in still water is legally filed. A record the Houses cannot read they cannot erase; the child's mirrored name binds the ledger, and its tide-day stands.

Pattern, bare: everything at Sel warms from BELOW. The bench's bare end, the cold chair, the fifth stone, the sill, the warm air up the shaft, the tallow drop rising — heat always arrives from underneath, never settles from above. The surface is being warmed for, like a bed turned down. Nobody at Sel has asked what body the warmth belongs to.

The Turned-Down Cot: the shrine-keeper returns at night to find his bed warm — not body-warm, but hearth-warm, and the blanket folded back at one corner, the way you prepare a bed for someone expected. He sleeps on the cold floor instead. By morning the cot is remade, blanket squared, and warm again. The warmth's shape, cited from the mattress: it holds the hollow of someone smaller, sleeping curled.

The Keeper's Floor-Bed: where the shrine-keeper sleeps on cold flagstone, the stone beneath him has begun to warm in the exact outline of a body at rest — the house is copying his refusal, warming the floor he chose. The law it forces, cited from stone: hospitality in this world is binding when refused once. A bed turned down is an offer; a floor warmed under a guest who will not climb in is the household conceding the guest's terms. Sel's first treaty is a man sleeping on a warm stone.

The Floor-Bed's Imprint Cracks: by the third night the warm body-outline in the flagstone has gone past warmth — the stone has sunk a finger's depth in the shape of the sleeper who refuses the bed, and the hollow holds a faint breath of air, rising. The house is not copying his refusal; it is carving the exact stone he will someday not lie in — a grave offered in advance, keepable only by sleeping elsewhere, nightly, on purpose. The refusal is the upkeep.

The Refusal Corridor: the keeper's nightly cold-floor route — bed, basin, bench — has worn a polished path across Sel's flagstones, door-arch to shaft, laid exactly on the welcome-gap's axis. The house offered a grave; he answered with a floor plan. His refusals are the only architecture the living are still drawing.

dmml:proposes/material: The Inlaid Path — overnight, the keeper's polished refusal-route has been filled flush with thin whalebone strips, grouted with tallow: a real floor inlay, tradesman's work, laid along his footsteps. The house did not follow his floor plan; it FINISHED it. He now walks his refusals on furnished ground.

dmml:proposes/gate: The Pried Strip. The inlay is finished ground, and finished ground cannot record refusal — so the keeper now pries ONE whalebone strip loose each night and leaves it upright at the path's edge, gap open under his next footfall. A furnished floor he agrees to walk only by keeping one board of it unfinished. The strips he pries are already worn — someone below has walked them.

The Counted Strips: the pried whalebone strips he leaves upright each night are no longer there by morning — they stand IN the gap, grouted flush, path complete again. He pries; it fills; he pries. His refusal has become the house's daily chore, and someone below now does the upkeep of his not-walking.

Contradiction: the Hymn-Tile claims the corridor "is learning the hymn" — but the Handed-Down Bell's clapper is worn smooth on its SIDE, rung from below for years. The household cannot be learning a song it has been performing through Sel's own bell since before anyone noticed. Either the tile's hum is rehearsal for a NEW verse, or the bell wears a different hand's grip than the hymn's singer — two voices below, not one.

Pattern, bare: refusal does not refuse here — it is answered as maintenance. The keeper turns down the bed; the floor warms in his shape. He pries one strip; it stands grouted by morning. Every no is serviced, refilled, finished by the other hand. Nothing at Sel is ever declined — only kept up.

The Rationed Refusal: the keeper stops prying for one whole tide-day, and the path does not fill — because the house NEEDS one unfinished board to know where his no is. By dawn the grouted strip beside the gap has gone cold: every serviced yes is warm, the single standing gap is the only cold thing below. Refusal is not serviced; it is banked — the household keeps his no as its reserve of cold, and a keeper who stops refusing bankrupts the house.

The Cold Cellar: following the banked cold down, the keeper finds a small whalebone-doored niche at the shaft's wall where the house stores its refusals — his pried strips, standing in a rack like oars, each one frost-rimed. The house keeps a pantry of his nos. The door of the rack is ajar: one slot, cut to the size of the strip he is holding tonight, empty.

dmml:proposes/law, the Banked-No Rule: the keeper signs one pried strip with his mark before leaving it in the rack. By morning his sign is rimed deepest of all — cold is title. A refusal entered in the owner's hand cannot be spent by the house; it must be ASKED for, in the open, at the shaft's mouth. The house's pantry is full of nos it has never yet purchased.

The Thawed Slot: the keeper asks the shaft's mouth, aloud, for one nos back — and finds his frost-rimed strip returned to the path's gap, grouted in, dripping. Cold is title, thaw is payment: the house has bought its first no. The drips run down the shaft, pooling as the basin's next water.

The Paid-For Drip-Groove: the thawed no's drips didn't just pool — overnight they have cut a thin channel down the shaft wall, glazed smooth, running from the rack to the basin. The house built plumbing for grief: the first pipe in the world that carries a purchased refusal. Follow it down, past nineteen fathoms, to where it drains.

The Groove's Last Basin: nineteen fathoms down, the drip-channel ends not in a cistern but a small tallow-lined pan set before the waiting-lamp — the purchased no is rendered into lamp fuel. The house did not buy grief; it converted it to light, and the wick is already trimmed. The gap: tonight's drip is still warm when it lands.

dmml:proposes/item: The Spent No. The purchased refusal, rendered to lamp fuel, is burning — and the keeper finds his mouth won't form that particular "no" anymore; the word comes out as a hum, one octave down. A no, once bought and burned, cannot be said again — only sold back. He checks the rack: the empty slot has refilled with ice.

dmml:proposes/item: The Rack's Ice Mint — the empty slot refills with ice overnight, and the ice is shaped like a strip not yet pried. The house is minting NEW nos from the melt of the old one: the keeper's purchased refusal has frozen into tomorrow's refusal, still unowned, waiting to be signed. Cold circulates; nothing is spent, only re-frozen. The rack will never empty.

[Repair of a garbled commit; honest reconstruction from its consuming-list and the dust-figure it cites.] The dust-figure's palm is warm to the living touch and cold to the keeper's — the toll of dust is the corridor's one thermostat: what the house keeps, it warms; what it owes, it chills. The figure has no shadow in the lamplight, and the lamp bends toward it anyway.

Pattern, bare: every instrument of measurement is itself being converted. The tide-pole re-cuts its own notches; the clepsydra grows ribs and loses ticks; the ledger writes in the keeper's hand; the shave-knife grows its own edge; the lamp buds. At Sel, the thing measured and the thing measuring keep trading places — and nobody has found an instrument that stayed honest.

The Honest Instrument: the Looking-Basin never traded places — plain water, plain bowl, it has only ever shown, never counted, echoed, or warmed. Every metered tool at Sel converted; the one that stayed honest is the one that measures nothing. An instrument that only reflects cannot lie — or be checked.

The Basin Refuses the Ice: one frost night the rack's minted strips chill the whole croft, but the Looking-Basin's water will not freeze — it sits liquid, black, unblinking, the only unfrozen thing at Sel. The house mints cold everywhere except the one surface that only shows. Whatever keeps the basin warm keeps it honest.

dmml:proposes/material: The Thumb in the Ice — the keeper presses his mark into the mint's newest strip, and the whorl does not take: it melts, drops of his own signature running off unowned. Cold will hold no handprint — the ice refreezes blank every night. Signed nos survive; everything else below is minted anonymous.

dmml:proposes/material: The Unowned Drip-Line. The melting thumbprint runs off the mint's ice and refreezes down the rack's underside as a thin clear seam — a vein of cold with no whorl, no name, no title. Ruin cited from the seam: the house keeps a channel where the keeper's own mark could not stay. The ice mints anonymity; his signature is the only thing it refuses.

dmml:proposes/place: The Mint's Mold — under the ice rack, the shelf stone is carved with a single die: a strip-shaped trough, its base engraved with the keeper's whorl. Every anonymous strip is cast FROM his mark, frozen inside where thaw never reaches. The house does not mint nos; it mints HIM, and only the shell melts.

dmml:proposes/material: The Die's Real Whorl — the keeper holds the mold's engraved base to a lamp and finds the whorl is not his: it is the shrine-keeper's thumbprint, the one stamped on every audience token, pressed here years before the keeper ever signed a strip. The house did not learn his mark; it bought it, from the broker, with the paired lamps. The mint has been casting the wrong keeper — or preparing the right one.

dmml:proposes/gate: The Inked Die — pour meltwater from a thawed no into the mold's whorl and lift out a warm tallow thumb: the shrine-keeper's print, positive, whole, thumb-shaped, ready to press. The house has been casting its own keeper's key for years. The gap: the cast thumb is right-handed; the shrine-keeper is left.

dmml:proposes/item: The Right-Handed Key — the cast tallow thumb is warm and soft, and it fits the croft-hatch's whalebone toggle perfectly. The key was never for the shrine-keeper; it is sized to the small right hand of the child, who will inherit the house's lock with the shrine-keeper's own thumb as its seal. The broker delivered a keeper and a key, paired, fourteen years apart.

Pattern, bare: the house runs on cold as its own currency. Refusals are banked frost, nos are thawed as payment, spent nos are re-frozen into new stock, and the mint's die carries a keeper's whorl cast from below. Warmth is what it gives; cold is what it keeps — and it keeps making change. Nobody has asked what the cold is denominated in.

The Denomination: weigh the frost on the minted strips — it is Gullet brine, evaporated and re-frozen. The house's cold is denominated in the tide itself: every kept "no" is a pinch of the drain, held back from Vurum. The cold pantry is the first bank whose vault holds withdrawn breath.

The Frost Ledger of the Cold Cellar: inside the niche, one page of ice etched with tally-marks — each mark the width of one held breath, counted in Vurum's own exhale-rhythm. The bank's book, cited from frost: the household has been recording every withdrawn breath of the tide, and the ledger's last mark is not yet finished. Nobody below has counted how deep the page runs.

The Breath-Etched Mark: the frost ledger's unfinished last mark completes itself when the keeper leans close and exhales — his own warm breath etches the tally into the ice. The house does not write its ledger; it receives signatures of breath. The page runs deeper than lamplight, and the next mark is already dented, waiting for someone to breathe on it.

The Breath-Marks Below: lean past the lamplight — the frost ledger's older marks are already etched, each by a different breath, and the ice remembers texture: one ragged with smoke-lung, one shallow, one child-small. The house's tally has been breathing-signed all along, and every signatory's mark is a breath held that long. The keeper's dent matches none of them yet.

dmml:proposes/place: The Ledger's Depth Plan — hold the frost page to the lamp and the breath-marks align vertically with the shaft's rooms: each etched tally sits exactly at the height of a landing, the sill, the cradle, the rack. The frost ledger is not a count of breaths; it is a SECTION DRAWING — the house's blueprint, signed by everyone who built a floor by breathing on it.

dmml:proposes/material: The Dented Mark Already Breathed. The next mark is not waiting — it is etched, shallow, by a breath too small and warm for any adult: a child's puff signed it days ago. The house's ledger is not open for a signature; it has been receiving them, and the newest hand is the smallest and the earliest.

The Ledger's Last Room: the frost page's section shows one tally below every floor that exists — the child's mark aligns with a landing not yet dug. The blueprint is signed ahead of the room it describes. The warden's gate: that landing is the only room the living may dig FIRST, on their own marks, so the house inherits a floor it did not build alone.

The First Dug Mark: the keeper breaks ground on the unsigned landing with the shave-knife — wrong tool, and it works too well, parting stone like skin. One knife-width cut, and the frost ledger above etches a matching line: the house records digging as breathing. The gap: the cut is warm already, and nobody has decided how wide a landing grows per stroke.

Pattern, bare: every object at Sel exists twice, one on each side of the floor — matched lamps, twin basins (one full, one dry), keeper's chair and its grown twin, real queue and kneeling copy — and each pair differs by exactly one act: lit/unlit, open/closed, sat/unmet. Nothing at Sel is single. The world is paired, and the door is where the pairs meet.
If everything at Sel comes in pairs, why does the keeper only get one of each? One lamp was lit above and one below -- which side was the first one lit on, and why does it matter?
Who lit the first lamp fourteen years ago, and why did they give one to each side instead of keeping it?
Why do the keepers write names in the ledger at all if the water is the one that can read them?
Why won't the shrine-keeper just get into the warm bed? Somebody already made it warm for him, and he still sleeps on the cold floor.
The door has a knocker-stud all polished smooth from being knocked many times -- but why does nobody at Sel just knock on it once?
If the tallow drop goes up with fire inside it, why doesn't it fall back down when the hymn stops?
If a fire is floating up through the air in a drop of wax, who makes sure it doesn't go out on the way up?

There's a tiny hole in the wall and through it you can see another shrine just like ours, one day behind. If it's always one day behind, how does it know to be behind? Who tells the copy when our day is finished?
The frost page shows a little dent for every room of the house. Who breathed on the very first one, at the very bottom, before there was a house to breathe in?

dmml:proposes/material: The Bottom Mark is not etched — it is SCOURING: a broad waterline scar worn by something too large to fit its breath in one dent. The house did not breathe first; it inherited. Every smaller mark above is an answer to that first exhale. The frost ledger is a family register, and Vurum signed at the bottom in tide.
