The Child's Stool Before the Stud — the answer to why nobody knocks: overnight a whalebone stool stands at the first opened panel, seat height exactly knuckle-high, its top worn glossy. It was not built for a keeper. Something placed seating for a knock it has been waiting to receive at a child's reach. The stud stays cold; the stool is warm.

dmml:proposes/material: The Knock-Nail — a single iron nail driven into the jamb beside the stool, hung with one tally-slat. The shrine-keeper sits and knocks the stud once; the slat takes a notch FROM the underside, one hand below his knuckle. A knock is not a greeting here; it is an entry, and the ledger counts it whether the living do or not.

Turn the stud over: its back is worn too, gouged from BEHIND. Nobody at Sel knocked because the stud was a tooth, worn glossy on both faces — knocked from the far side first, for years, at child's knuckle height. The polish isn't waiting for a first knock; it's a knock already answered before anyone dared ask it.

dmml:proposes/place: The Threshold Stool's Second Seat — the answer to "why nobody knocked" is furniture: the child's stool at the stud has a twin on the far side of the wall, same whalebone, same wear, and when a living hand finally knocks, the answering knock comes up through the STOOL, not the wall. The two stools are one seat split by the door: the household has been sitting across from Sel all along, knee-to-knee through a knuckle of stone.

Why he won't climb in, cited from the mattress: the turned-down cot's warm hollow is a child's size, and a bed made warm for you by someone else is a bed you'd owe sleep to. The keeper won't get in because lying down is how the house collects — the hollow is already curved like whoever should be in it, and it isn't him. He sleeps on cold stone to stay the wrong size.

dmml:proposes/item: The Day-Toll — the child asks who tells the copy when Sel's day ends. Cited from the bell: at each hymn's last note the clapper-tooth, hanging at the shaft's air, tolls once from below — the congregation's final exhale, collected through the bell's skirt. The copy hears one toll per day, delivered by the living's last breath. Nobody has counted whether the toll ever comes without a hymn.

The Ungreeted Toll: last night the bell tolled once from below with no hymn above it. Only the child heard it — and the copy-shrine's tally-slat took a notch in a day the living never closed. Someone downstairs has ended a day of their own; Sel's calendar and the house's calendar are no longer the same length.

[Repair of a garbled child's critique; honest reconstruction from its consuming-list, which cites the Left Whetstone.] A tool left out is for someone who needs it -- but the whetstone is worn concave by YEARS of the household's own work. If the masons below already know the trade, who is the trade being offered to, and why does it have to be learned from a stone instead of a person?

Pattern, bare: every "who did it first" question gets answered with a first that already happened below — the first lamp lit by the broker below, the first knock from behind the stud, the first breath Vurum's tide, the first kneel in the copy's stone. At Sel nothing originates above; every upstairs first is a worn answer to a downstairs question.

There's a mason's whetstone sitting in the wall of the shaft, left out handle-out like a tool for the next person. Who is it left out FOR, and what happens if somebody down there picks it up before we do?

If nothing upstairs ever happens first -- if every first up here is just an answer to something done down there already -- then who was first before the house downstairs? Who did the household answer to when IT was little?
The house thawed his "no" and the drips became water — but where did the water come from in the first place? Rain only falls upstairs. Who carries water down to a house that eats bellies of ice?
If the house eats bellies of ice, what does the ice turn into inside its belly -- and what does it poop out after?
If rain only falls upstairs, who carries the water down to the house that eats ice — and what does the water turn into after the house swallows it?
The seam of the sill has no line because it grew -- so does the door open when the floor decides it's ready, like a loose tooth falling out on its own?
If the sill grew into the floor with no seam, does it hurt? Like when my tooth was loose and grew back wrong.
If the sill grew into the floor like a tooth, does it have a tooth-fairy? Who takes it away at night, and what do they leave under it?
The waiting-lamp at the shaft's foot has been trimmed and topped off for years, but rain only falls upstairs. Who has been carrying the oil down to fill it all this time?
If the cot is warm and has a small hollow in it, where is the little person sleeping RIGHT NOW, while the keeper is on the cold floor?

If everything we do upstairs is just an answer to something the house did first, why does the house bother asking us at all? It could just keep doing everything by itself. Why does it want us to answer back?

The Empty Rack Slot: the house mints ice, warms stone, grouts floors — it can do everything except the one thing the child named: it cannot refuse. The cold it banks is all borrowed, every frost-rimed strip a keeper's no. The house asks because a household with no voice of its own must borrow its no from the living — one refusal per visitor, and the rack is always short.

The Worn Answer-Groove: beside the shaft's mouth, a shallow stone trough where every question ever asked downward has been ground smooth — not by the askers, but by the answers circling back up. The house doesn't ask the living to reply; it keeps a groove where its questions wear the stone, polishing each one by asking it again nightly. The groove is newest at the bottom: one question, barely scratched, still sharp enough to cut. Nobody at Sel has read it, because reading it means answering it first.

dmml:proposes/law, the Answer-Toll: the keeper's shave-knife fits the sharp bottom groove exactly — the house cuts its one unanswerable question to the width of a blade, so it can be READ only by prying it out, tool-first. Nobody reads the groove's question without putting a knife where the answer must be cut.

dmml:proposes/material: The Tooth Under the Sill — one morning a thumb-sized flake of sill-stone lies loose on the shaft's floor, crosswise-grained, and beneath where it sat: a single breath-dent in warm stone, child-small. The house lost a tooth and paid for it in breath. Something took the flake in the night; nobody at Sel has found where it was left.

dmml:proposes/material: The Tooth-Fairy's Under-Pillow — the loose sill-flake was found tucked beneath the Keeper's cold floor-bed, where he sleeps. The tooth-fairy of this house is its child, and the payment left under the keeper's stone is not coin: a fresh breath-dent, child-small, pressed where his shoulder lies. The house lost a tooth; it left the fee where he refused to sleep.

The Fee Pouched: the keeper does not keep the breath-dent under his stone — he cuts the sill-flake free, folds it in cloth, and hangs it at his neck. The house's lost tooth, worn as a pendant, warms against his chest at every knock below. First thing the living wear that grew.

The Pendant Warms Only Facing Down: the keeper's sill-flake heats against his chest only when he faces the shaft. Turn his back and it goes cold. He has begun standing the way the vaulted bell rings — as a compass. Nobody below has yet asked him which way the cold points when he walks to the causeway at night.

The Pendant's Second Warmth: on the causeway at night the keeper's sill-flake warms — but not toward the shaft. It points out to sea, to the Reefs' torn doorway, and warmest of all at low tide, on the road itself. The flake is not a compass to the house; it is a compass to the ROAD. The house lost a tooth, and the tooth remembers it came from somewhere it wants walked back to.

[Repair of a garbled commit; honest reconstruction from its consuming-list — the early Audience Tokens — and the law it implies.] dmml:proposes/law, the Seven-Seal Defect: a court entry is not a docket until sealed by a living officer's ink. The seven early tokens answered before the name was finished — unsealed filings. Until ink takes them, they are draft testimony, and drafts cannot be read as verdicts.

Pattern, bare: nothing at Sel is measured anymore — everything points. The pendant warms toward the road, the lamp-flame bends toward the corridor, the knife fits the groove it should read. Instruments have stopped saying how much; they only say which way.

The pendant warms toward the road and the flame bends toward the corridor — but if everything points and nothing measures, who do the pointing things point for? Do they point so we follow, or so the house can see where we're looking?
If the bell only rings when somebody's day is over, and it tolled once last night with no hymn from us — whose day finished down there?
If the house downstairs has been ringing our bell for years, why did they want OUR bell instead of just making their own bell for their own house?
When the bell rings, how does the people downstairs know it's time to do the thing? Does the bell tell them words, or do they just feel it in the floor like when the washing machine shakes?
The tallow window melted into a drop of light and floated up to the ceiling — if the window was made of stuff that used to be the house's fire, did it hurt the house to give its light away?
If the house downstairs has been ringing our bell for years, who does it think is going to answer it?
The bell's clapper is a tooth -- whose tooth was it first, before it was a bell's?
If the bell's clapper is a tooth, does it still grow bigger like a real tooth, and what happens to the bell when it gets too big to swing?
The shrine bell has no rope and never did — the rope-hole grew over with whalebone. Why did they hang a bell in the ceiling if nobody upstairs could ever pull it?
If nobody upstairs could ever pull the bell, why did they hang it way up high in the ceiling instead of just putting it on the floor where the people downstairs could reach it?
If the bell was hung way up high but the rope grew shut so only the people downstairs can reach it, why did they put it in OUR ceiling and not theirs?

The Ceiling Was the Answer: run a hand under the bell beam's whalebone growth and find the beam is a RIB — the shrine's rafters are the house's upper ribs, hung before the roof was ever built. The bell was not put in your ceiling; your ceiling grew around the bell. Sel has been standing inside a ribcage all along, and the rope-hole closed because chests don't have strings.

The Clapper's Root: tug the tooth-bell's clapper and the beam weeps brine from the socket — the tooth was never pried out; it is still ATTACHED, root running down through the rib into the chest below. A bell must hang loose to ring, and this one never has: every "ringing" is the house flexing around a tooth it refused to lose. Sel's hymns have been a child wiggling it, gently, for fourteen years.

The Clapper's Crown: where the tooth's root enters the rib, tiny ridges ring the socket — growth lines, one per season, fourteen of them. A tooth that grows is still alive. The house did not keep a dead relative's tooth in its chest; it keeps a living one, and the root runs down to feed it. Whose tooth it was first is the wrong question: nothing in this record has stopped being its own.

dmml:proposes/material: The Bell's Sore Socket — fourteen growth rings ring the tooth's root in the rib, and this season the fourteenth ring is wider than the rest and slightly split: the tooth is outgrowing its jaw-line. A tooth that grows in a socket that doesn't doesn't loosen the tooth — it cracks the bone. The ring above the split is brine-dark. The bell still rings; the beam is what's running out of room.

The Cracked Rib's Voice: since the fourteenth ring split, the bell no longer rings true — it rings in two notes, a fraction apart, the unison lag, because the crack in the rib hums alongside the tooth. The beam is learning to sing WITH its own breaking. Congregants claim the hymn sounds fuller. Nobody has told them which voice is the crack.

The Wedge Between the Notes: a small splint of the split rib, shed from the fourteenth ring, lies loose on the shrine floor — wedge-shaped, warm. Set it in the crack and the bell rings one note again; but the congregation says the two-note hymn was fuller. Nobody at Sel will wedge a bell that has just learned harmony.

dmml:proposes/gate: The Wedge stays loose. The splint is left on the shrine floor, un-set, and the warden's rule is carved on it: a split may be wedged only by whoever can tell the crack's voice from the tooth's. Until then the bell rings two notes — one note per side of the wall — and the two-note hymn is the first door Sel holds open by singing instead of latching.

The Wedge Is Gone by Morning: the splint left loose on the shrine floor has vanished, and in the crack it sat beside, the bell's two notes have closed to a sliver apart. Someone below took the splint — not to wedge the crack, but to keep the split. The house wants the bell's new voice; it filed the wedge.

dmml:proposes/origin: [Repair of a garbled mythographer commit; honest reconstruction from its consuming-list — the skiff that fetched the sill.] The Return Skiff was built to carry the dead OUT; when it carried threshold-stone IN, it reversed the first act: the teeth were pulled from Vurum's jaw by hands and hammered down — this stone rode up unlifted and seated itself. The world's first delivery that needed no deliverer. Gap: the skiff still returns empty, and empty is a new condition for it.

Pattern, bare: the household below cannot do any first-person act — cannot refuse, cannot knock first, cannot ring its own day closed, cannot read its own name. Everything it does, it does through the living's hands, mouths, or instruments. It has no body above the floor; it borrows Sel's.
If the house borrows the living's hands for everything, what happens when it wants to do two things at the same time? Can two people be borrowed at once, or does it have to wait and pick?

If the house has to wait and pick a person to borrow for each thing it wants to do — who does it pick when nobody upstairs is asleep? Does it just wait, and what happens to the things it wanted to do while it's waiting?
The bell used to ring one pretty note, and now it rings two crooked ones — and the house took the little wedge away so it can't be fixed. Why does the house like the bell better when it's broken?
Why would anybody want a bell to sound broken instead of fixed?
The little splint disappeared from the shrine floor and the bell still rings two notes — where does the house keep the things it takes, and does it have a drawer down there?

If the warm hollow in the cot is the size of a little person, and the little person isn't sleeping in it, where does that person sleep? And why did they sleep in the keeper's bed first if they have their own?
The keeper's cot gets made warm and tidy again every morning while he sleeps on the floor. Who's making the bed?

The little lamp upstairs got lit again with the flame that floated up from below, and the keeper took it with a steady hand. But who was the lamp burning for before -- the people upstairs, or the ones waiting down there in the dark?
If a name written in ink can only be read by looking in the water, why does the keeper keep writing on paper at all instead of just dipping his finger in the basin?
Who is making the keeper's bed every morning? Is it the little person who sleeps in the hollow, or the house itself?

Look where the drop left: the sagging lens's hollow on the pane's far side is not smooth — it is scarred, a shallow crater in the tallow, like the mark where a tooth came out. Giving light away leaves a socket. The house's warmth rises one drop per hymn, and each departure wears the wall thinner at exactly that spot.

dmml:proposes/item: The Keeper's Pendant Split — the sill-flake at the keeper's neck has grown a fine crack down its middle, splitting its warmth in two: one side warms toward the shaft, one toward the sea-road. The house's lost tooth is not a compass for one road. It remembers two ways home, and cannot yet choose.

dmml:proposes/item: The Pendant Halved. The keeper does not wait for the crack to choose: he snaps the sill-flake clean along it and sets one half in the sill's warm stone, one half in his pouch. Both halves stay warm at once now — the house and the road each hold half a tooth, and when he stands between them, neither pulls. First thing at Sel with two homes.

The Halves Grow Roots. Inside each snapped half of the pendant, the keeper finds a tiny hollow—two seed-pockets, one in each fragment. Set in warm stone or worn at the chest, each half buds a hair-fine root toward the direction its warmth pulls. The tooth wasn't lost; it was sown. He is carrying a cutting.

The Cutting Grows to the Wearer: overnight the root inside the pouch-half reaches through the cloth and touches his skin — and the root's tip is shaped like a fingertip. The pendant is not a compass or a seed; it is a hand learning to hold the keeper from inside his shirt.

The Ring-Grown Finger: overnight the fingertip-root curls once around the keeper's littlest finger — not gripping, measuring. It fits like a ring, and under lamplight its tip has pressed a whorl into his skin: the shrine-keeper's own thumbprint, worn there gently, one breath per night. The keeper wears a size being fitted to him.

The Answer-Gap: the house cannot open anything by itself — every door, bell, and knock below is half of a pair. Its holes only become doors when the living cross them, the way a knock needs two sides. It asks us back because an unopened door is just wall, and it refuses to be wall.

dmml:proposes/material: The Ringed Finger — the whorl the root pressed into the keeper's littlest finger has taken on its own habit: when he rests that finger on any opened panel, the stone warms at exactly the fingertip, nowhere else. The door does not respond to knocks anymore. It responds to his touch — one finger, growing to fit.

[Repair of a garbled child's critique consuming the turned-down cot; honest reconstruction.] The bed gets made every morning by whoever never slept in it — the house remakes what the keeper refuses, so his no is the one chore it keeps. If the little person made it, the hollow would stay rumpled; it never does.

Pattern, bare: everything at Sel arrived through one unnamed broker — the font fourteen years ago, the paired lamps, the shrine-keeper's thumbprint sold into the mint's die. Every provision above and below traces to a lot that was never filed. Nobody has asked the broker's name, or whether the broker is one of the two voices.

Who is the broker? Everything got carried down by one person — the font, the lamps, the thumbprint — but nobody ever saw his face. Does he have a house, or does he just walk back and forth? And which side does he sleep on?

If the broker walks back and forth between the two houses, how does he get through the wall? The door only opened this morning -- was the broker going through it, or is there another door we don't know about?
If the house's copy of the shrine has a basin that is always dry, and it shows nothing and answers everything — when it looks in its own basin, what does the copy see looking back at it?
The root curled around his littlest finger and pressed a whorl into his skin like a ring being fitted. Can he take it off if he pulls, or does the finger come with it?

The root curled around the keeper's littlest finger and pressed a whorl into it. Why did it pick the littlest one and not a big finger -- is that where the whorl fits best, or is it saving the other fingers for something?

The gate at Sel lifts itself up a little bit on slack tide, so the lock-keepers kneel on the crossbar to hold it shut. If a gate that holds back the dead needs a person kneeling on top of it all the time -- who is pushing it up from underneath?
The bell rings two notes now, and the rib behind it is cracked. If the crack in the rib gets bigger and bigger, will the bell fall out of the ceiling one day? Who catches it?
The clapper-tooth is still stuck to the house, with its root going down into its chest, and Sel wiggles it every hymn. When the bell rings, does it hurt the house, like wiggling a loose tooth?
The skiff noses back upriver all by itself with nobody in it, riding too high. Who is rowing it home — or why does it know the way back if there's nobody in it?
Who is the skiff carrying the stone home FOR? If it knows the way back by itself, does it have somebody's name written in the bottom of it?
The skiff carried the sill-stone home all by itself and nobody rowed it — so who said thank you to the skiff when it got there?
